topics.name: Unit 1: Polynomial and Rational Functions
topics.description: Explore polynomial and rational functions, their rates of change, zeros, end behavior, asymptotes, holes, transformations, and modeling applications. This unit covers 30-40% of the AP Precalculus Exam.

concepts.title: Change in Tandem
concepts.content_html:
Change in Tandem

Functions describe how two quantities change together. When one quantity changes, the other responds in a predictable way. Understanding this relationship is the foundation of precalculus.

What Is a Function?

A function is a relationship where each input value produces exactly one output value. We write \( f(x) \) to denote the output of function \( f \) for input \( x \).

Domain and Range

The domain of a function is the set of all possible input values. The range is the set of all possible output values. For example, if \( f(x) = \sqrt{x} \), the domain is \( x \geq 0 \) and the range is \( f(x) \geq 0 \).

Increasing and Decreasing Functions

A function is strictly increasing on an interval if, for any two values \( a \) and \( b \) in that interval with \( a < b \), we have \( f(a) < f(b) \). Similarly, a function is strictly decreasing if \( a < b \) implies \( f(a) > f(b) \).

Key Idea: When we say a function is increasing or decreasing on the AP Precalculus exam, we always mean strictly increasing or decreasing.

Concavity

Concavity describes how the rate of change itself is changing. A function is concave up when its rate of change is increasing (the graph curves upward like a cup). A function is concave down when its rate of change is decreasing (the graph curves downward like a frown).

Zeros of a Function

A zero (or root) of a function is an input value \( x \) where \( f(x) = 0 \). Graphically, zeros are the \( x \)-intercepts of the function.

Worked Example

Consider the function \( f(x) = x^2 - 4 \).

  • Domain: All real numbers \( (-\infty, \infty) \)
  • Range: \( [-4, \infty) \)
  • Zeros: Set \( x^2 - 4 = 0 \), so \( x = -2 \) or \( x = 2 \)
  • Decreasing: on \( (-\infty, 0) \) because as \( x \) increases, \( f(x) \) decreases
  • Increasing: on \( (0, \infty) \) because as \( x \) increases, \( f(x) \) increases
  • Concavity: Concave up everywhere (the parabola opens upward)
AP Exam Tip: Always describe where a function is increasing or decreasing using intervals of the input (\( x \)-values), not output values.

problems.question_html: The function \( g(x) = -x^2 + 6x - 5 \) models the height of a ball in meters after \( x \) seconds. On which interval is \( g \) strictly increasing?

hints.text: Find the vertex of the parabola. The function increases to the left of the vertex.
The vertex is at \( x = \frac{-6}{2(-1)} = 3 \). The function increases on \( (-\infty, 3) \).

solution_steps.text: The vertex of \( g(x) = -x^2 + 6x - 5 \) is at \( x = \frac{-b}{2a} = \frac{-6}{2(-1)} = 3 \).
Since the parabola opens downward (\( a = -1 < 0 \)), the function is strictly increasing on \( (-\infty, 3) \) and strictly decreasing on \( (3, \infty) \).

problems.question_html: A function \( f \) has domain \( [-3, 7] \) and range \( [-2, 10] \). Which of the following is true?

choices.text: \( f \) must be increasing on its entire domain

hints.text: Think about what domain and range tell you about possible inputs and outputs.
The range is \( [-2, 10] \), so all outputs are between \( -2 \) and \( 10 \). The value 15 is outside this range.

solution_steps.text: The range \( [-2, 10] \) means all output values of \( f \) satisfy \( -2 \leq f(x) \leq 10 \).
Since \( 15 > 10 \), the output \( f(x) = 15 \) is impossible. The other options are not guaranteed by the given information.

problems.question_html: The function \( h(x) = x^3 \) is strictly increasing on its entire domain. What are the zeros of \( h \)?

hints.text: A zero is an input where the output equals 0.
Set \( x^3 = 0 \). What value of \( x \) satisfies this?

solution_steps.text: The only solution is \( x = 0 \). This is the only zero of \( h \).

problems.question_html: A function \( f \) is concave up on an interval. This means the rate of change of \( f \) is __________ on that interval.

hints.text: Think about what concave up looks like: the curve bends upward like a cup.
When a function is concave up, the slope gets steeper (more positive or less negative), meaning the rate of change is increasing.

solution_steps.text: Concave up means the graph curves upward. This happens when the slope of the function gets larger as you move from left to right.
Therefore, the rate of change is increasing on a concave-up interval.

problems.question_html: The function \( f(x) = \frac{1}{x - 2} \) has which domain?

hints.text: The domain excludes any input that makes the denominator zero.
The denominator \( x - 2 = 0 \) when \( x = 2 \). Every other real number is in the domain.

solution_steps.text: A rational function is undefined wherever its denominator equals zero.
Setting \( x - 2 = 0 \) gives \( x = 2 \). The domain is all real numbers except \( x = 2 \).

problems.question_html: A continuous function \( f \) has \( f(-1) = 3 \) and \( f(4) = -2 \). Which statement must be true?

choices.text: \( f \) has a zero between \( x = -1 \) and \( x = 4 \)
\( f \) has a maximum at \( x = -1 \)

hints.text: Notice that \( f(-1) > 0 \) and \( f(4) < 0 \). What theorem applies to continuous functions?
By the Intermediate Value Theorem, since \( f \) is continuous and changes sign, there must be a zero between \( x = -1 \) and \( x = 4 \).

solution_steps.text: Since \( f(-1) = 3 > 0 \) and \( f(4) = -2 < 0 \), the function changes sign on the interval \( [-1, 4] \).
Because \( f \) is continuous, the Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees at least one value \( c \) in \( (-1, 4) \) where \( f(c) = 0 \).

problems.question_html: The graph of a function \( f \) is concave down on \( (1, 5) \) and concave up on \( (5, 9) \). The point \( x = 5 \) is called a point of __________.

hints.text: What do we call a point where concavity changes?
When a function changes from concave down to concave up (or vice versa), the transition point is called a point of inflection.

solution_steps.text: At \( x = 5 \), the concavity changes from concave down to concave up.
A point where the concavity of a function changes is called a point of inflection.

problems.question_html: A function \( p \) is defined on \( [-5, 5] \). Given that \( p(-5) = 2 \), \( p(0) = -3 \), and \( p(5) = 2 \), how many zeros does \( p \) have at minimum if \( p \) is continuous?

hints.text: Look at where the function changes sign. Each sign change guarantees at least one zero.
\( p(-5) = 2 > 0 \) and \( p(0) = -3 < 0 \): sign change on \( (-5, 0) \). Also \( p(0) = -3 < 0 \) and \( p(5) = 2 > 0 \): sign change on \( (0, 5) \). That gives at least 2 zeros.

solution_steps.text: Between \( x = -5 \) and \( x = 0 \), the function goes from \( 2 \) (positive) to \( -3 \) (negative). By the IVT, there is at least one zero in \( (-5, 0) \).
Between \( x = 0 \) and \( x = 5 \), the function goes from \( -3 \) (negative) to \( 2 \) (positive). By the IVT, there is at least one zero in \( (0, 5) \).
Therefore, \( p \) has at least 2 zeros.

problems.question_html:
A company tracks its daily revenue \( R(t) \) (in thousands of dollars) over a 10-day period, where \( t \) is the number of days since the start.

\( t \)0246810
\( R(t) \)58101111.511.8

(a) Identify the domain and range of \( R \) based on the table.

(b) Is \( R \) increasing, decreasing, or neither on \( [0, 10] \)? Justify your answer.

(c) Based on the pattern of outputs, is \( R \) concave up or concave down on \( [0, 10] \)? Explain your reasoning.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) Domain: {0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10} (or [0, 10] if R is continuous). Range: {5, 8, 10, 11, 11.5, 11.8} (or [5, 11.8]).
(b) R is strictly increasing on [0, 10] because as t increases, R(t) increases at every pair of consecutive data points.
(c) R is concave down. The rate of change decreases: from t=0 to t=2, the increase is 3; from t=2 to t=4, the increase is 2; from t=4 to t=6, the increase is 1; from t=6 to t=8, the increase is 0.5; from t=8 to t=10, the increase is 0.3. Since the successive increases are getting smaller, the rate of change is decreasing, which means concave down.

hints.text: For (c), compute the change in \( R \) over each 2-day interval and look at whether those changes are getting larger or smaller.
The changes are \( 3, 2, 1, 0.5, 0.3 \). Since these are decreasing, the rate of change is decreasing, which means concave down.

solution_steps.text: (a) The domain from the table is \( \{0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10\} \). The range is \( \{5, 8, 10, 11, 11.5, 11.8\} \).
(b) As \( t \) increases through each pair of consecutive values, \( R(t) \) also increases: \( 5 < 8 < 10 < 11 < 11.5 < 11.8 \). So \( R \) is strictly increasing.

(c) The successive changes in \( R \) are: \( 8-5=3 \), \( 10-8=2 \), \( 11-10=1 \), \( 11.5-11=0.5 \), \( 11.8-11.5=0.3 \). These changes are decreasing, meaning the rate of change is decreasing. Therefore \( R \) is concave down.

problems.question_html:
A runner's distance from the starting line, \( d(t) \) in meters, is recorded at several times \( t \) in seconds:

\( t \)036912
\( d(t) \)010254570

(a) Is \( d \) strictly increasing on \( [0, 12] \)? Justify your answer using the data.

(b) Compute the changes in \( d \) over each 3-second interval. What do these values tell you about the concavity of \( d \)?

(c) The runner claims she was running at a constant speed. Does the data support this claim? Explain.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) Yes, d is strictly increasing. For every pair of consecutive t-values, d(t) increases: 0 < 10 < 25 < 45 < 70.
(b) The changes are: 10-0=10, 25-10=15, 45-25=20, 70-45=25. These changes are increasing, so the rate of change is increasing, which means d is concave up.
(c) No. A constant speed would produce equal changes in distance over equal time intervals. The changes (10, 15, 20, 25) are not equal; they are increasing. The runner is accelerating, not running at constant speed.

hints.text: For (c), think about what constant speed means in terms of equal distances over equal time intervals.
Constant speed means equal distance changes: the changes are \( 10, 15, 20, 25 \), which are not equal. The runner is speeding up.

solution_steps.text: (a) Yes. Checking consecutive values: \( d(0) = 0 < d(3) = 10 < d(6) = 25 < d(9) = 45 < d(12) = 70 \). Each output is greater than the previous, so \( d \) is strictly increasing.
(b) Changes over each 3-second interval: \( 10, 15, 20, 25 \). These are increasing, so the rate of change is increasing, indicating \( d \) is concave up.

(c) Constant speed requires equal distance changes over equal time intervals. Since \( 10 
eq 15 
eq 20 
eq 25 \), the runner is not at constant speed. She is accelerating.

concepts.title: Rates of Change
concepts.content_html:
Rates of Change

The rate of change of a function measures how quickly the output changes relative to the input. This idea connects algebra to calculus and is central to the AP Precalculus course.

Average Rate of Change

The average rate of change (AROC) of a function \( f \) over the interval \( [a, b] \) is:

\[ \text{AROC} = \frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a} \]

This is the slope of the secant line connecting the points \( (a, f(a)) \) and \( (b, f(b)) \) on the graph of \( f \).

Approximating the Rate of Change at a Point

To approximate the rate of change at a specific point \( x = c \), compute the average rate of change over a small interval containing \( c \). The smaller the interval, the better the approximation.

For example, to approximate the rate of change of \( f \) at \( x = 3 \), you might compute:

\[ \frac{f(3.01) - f(3)}{3.01 - 3} \quad \text{or} \quad \frac{f(3.1) - f(2.9)}{3.1 - 2.9} \]

Comparing Rates of Change

Comparing the average rate of change over different intervals reveals how the function behaves. If the AROC is increasing over successive intervals, the function is concave up. If the AROC is decreasing, the function is concave down.

Worked Example

Let \( f(x) = x^2 \). Find the average rate of change on \( [1, 4] \).

\[ \text{AROC} = \frac{f(4) - f(1)}{4 - 1} = \frac{16 - 1}{3} = \frac{15}{3} = 5 \]

This means on average, \( f(x) \) increases by 5 units for each 1-unit increase in \( x \) over the interval \( [1, 4] \).

Key Idea: The average rate of change is the slope of the secant line. It gives a linear approximation of how the function behaves over an interval.
AP Exam Tip: Always include units when computing average rate of change in context problems. A rate of change without units is incomplete.

problems.question_html: What is the average rate of change of \( f(x) = 3x + 2 \) on the interval \( [1, 5] \)?

hints.text: Use the formula: AROC = \( \frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a} \).
\( f(5) = 17 \), \( f(1) = 5 \). AROC = \( \frac{17 - 5}{5 - 1} = \frac{12}{4} = 3 \). For a linear function, the AROC always equals the slope.

solution_steps.text: AROC = \( \frac{17 - 5}{5 - 1} = \frac{12}{4} = 3 \). This equals the slope of the linear function.

problems.question_html: The temperature \( T(h) \) in degrees Fahrenheit at hour \( h \) is recorded as: \( T(2) = 58 \) and \( T(8) = 76 \). What is the average rate of change of temperature from \( h = 2 \) to \( h = 8 \)?

hints.text: AROC = change in temperature divided by change in time.
\( \frac{76 - 58}{8 - 2} = \frac{18}{6} = 3 \) degrees per hour.

solution_steps.text: The temperature increases at an average rate of 3 degrees Fahrenheit per hour.

problems.question_html: Find the average rate of change of \( f(x) = x^2 \) on \( [2, 5] \).

hints.text: Use the AROC formula with \( f(2) \) and \( f(5) \).

problems.question_html: The average rate of change of \( g(x) \) on \( [3, 7] \) is \( -4 \). If \( g(3) = 20 \), find \( g(7) \).

hints.text: Use the AROC formula and solve for \( g(7) \).

solution_steps.text: Multiply both sides by 4: \( g(7) - 20 = -16 \), so \( g(7) = 4 \).

problems.question_html: The function \( f(x) = x^3 - 3x \) has average rates of change of \( -2 \) on \( [0, 1] \) and \( 4 \) on \( [1, 2] \). What does this tell you about the function near \( x = 1 \)?

choices.text: The function has a zero at \( x = 1 \)
The function changes from decreasing to increasing near \( x = 1 \)
The function is concave down near \( x = 1 \)
The function has no special behavior near \( x = 1 \)

hints.text: A negative AROC suggests the function is decreasing, and a positive AROC suggests it is increasing.
The AROC goes from \( -2 \) (decreasing) to \( 4 \) (increasing). This sign change in the rate suggests a local minimum near \( x = 1 \), where the function transitions from decreasing to increasing.

solution_steps.text: On \( [0, 1] \), the AROC is \( -2 \), indicating \( f \) is generally decreasing on that interval.
On \( [1, 2] \), the AROC is \( 4 \), indicating \( f \) is generally increasing.
The change from negative to positive average rate of change tells us the function transitions from decreasing to increasing near \( x = 1 \), suggesting a local minimum.

problems.question_html: For \( f(x) = \sqrt{x} \), which interval has the greater average rate of change?

choices.text: Both intervals have the same average rate of change
Cannot be determined without a calculator

hints.text: Compute the AROC on each interval separately and compare.

solution_steps.text: Since \( \frac{1}{3} > \frac{1}{5} \), the interval \( [1, 4] \) has the greater average rate of change. This makes sense because \( \sqrt{x} \) is concave down, so its rate of change decreases.

problems.question_html: Find the average rate of change of \( f(x) = 2x^2 - 3x + 1 \) on \( [1, 4] \).

hints.text: Evaluate \( f(1) \) and \( f(4) \), then use the AROC formula.

problems.question_html: The average rate of change of a function \( f \) on \( [0, 2] \) is 5, on \( [2, 4] \) is 5, and on \( [4, 6] \) is 5. What type of function could \( f \) be?

hints.text: What kind of function has the same average rate of change over every equal-length interval?
A constant AROC over all intervals of equal length is the defining property of a linear function.

solution_steps.text: The AROC is 5 on every interval \( [0,2] \), \( [2,4] \), and \( [4,6] \). This means the rate of change is constant.
A function with a constant rate of change is a linear function (e.g., \( f(x) = 5x + c \) for some constant \( c \)).

problems.question_html:
A population of bacteria, \( P(t) \), is measured at several times \( t \) (in hours):

\( t \)01234
\( P(t) \)100150225337506

(a) Find the average rate of change of \( P \) on \( [0, 2] \) and on \( [2, 4] \). Include units.

(b) Is the average rate of change of \( P \) increasing or decreasing over successive intervals? What does this tell you about the concavity of \( P \)?

(c) Use the average rate of change on \( [3, 4] \) to approximate \( P(3.5) \).
problems.correct_answer:
(a) AROC on [0,2] = (225-100)/(2-0) = 62.5 bacteria per hour. AROC on [2,4] = (506-225)/(4-2) = 140.5 bacteria per hour.
(b) The AROC is increasing (62.5 then 140.5), so the rate of growth is accelerating. This means P is concave up.
(c) AROC on [3,4] = (506-337)/(4-3) = 169 bacteria per hour. P(3.5) is approximately P(3) + 169(0.5) = 337 + 84.5 = 421.5 bacteria.

hints.text: For (c), use the secant line from \( t = 3 \) to \( t = 4 \) as a linear approximation.

solution_steps.text: (a) AROC on \( [0,2] = \frac{225 - 100}{2 - 0} = \frac{125}{2} = 62.5 \) bacteria per hour. AROC on \( [2,4] = \frac{506 - 225}{4 - 2} = \frac{281}{2} = 140.5 \) bacteria per hour.
(b) The AROC increases from 62.5 to 140.5 over successive intervals. An increasing rate of change means \( P \) is concave up.
(c) AROC on \( [3,4] = \frac{506 - 337}{1} = 169 \). Using this to approximate: \( P(3.5) \approx 337 + 169(0.5) = 421.5 \) bacteria.

problems.question_html:
A car's position \( s(t) \) (in miles) at time \( t \) (in hours) is given by \( s(t) = t^2 + 2t \).

(a) Find the average rate of change (average velocity) on \( [1, 3] \). Include units.

(b) Approximate the instantaneous rate of change (velocity) at \( t = 2 \) by computing the AROC on \( [1.9, 2.1] \).

(c) Compare your answers from (a) and (b). Why are they different?
problems.correct_answer:
(a) s(3) = 9+6 = 15, s(1) = 1+2 = 3. AROC = (15-3)/(3-1) = 12/2 = 6 miles per hour.
(b) s(2.1) = 4.41+4.2 = 8.61. s(1.9) = 3.61+3.8 = 7.41. AROC = (8.61-7.41)/(2.1-1.9) = 1.2/0.2 = 6 miles per hour.
(c) In this case the answers are the same because s(t) is quadratic and t=2 is the midpoint of [1,3]. For quadratics, the AROC over [a,b] equals the instantaneous rate at the midpoint. In general, the AROC gives an average over a wider interval while the approximation at a point uses a small interval to better estimate the rate at that specific moment.

hints.text: For (b), evaluate \( s \) at \( t = 1.9 \) and \( t = 2.1 \), then use the AROC formula.

solution_steps.text: (c) Both give 6 mph. For a quadratic \( s(t) = t^2 + 2t \), the AROC on \( [a, b] \) equals the instantaneous rate at the midpoint \( \frac{a+b}{2} \). Here \( t = 2 \) is the midpoint of \( [1, 3] \), so the answers match.

concepts.title: Rates of Change in Linear and Quadratic Functions
concepts.content_html:
Rates of Change in Linear and Quadratic Functions

Linear and quadratic functions have distinctive rate-of-change properties that make them easy to identify from data or graphs.

Linear Functions: Constant Rate of Change

A linear function \( f(x) = mx + b \) has a constant rate of change equal to its slope \( m \). No matter which interval you choose, the average rate of change is always \( m \).

This means:

  • The AROC is the same on every interval of the same length
  • The graph is a straight line with slope \( m \)
  • The output changes by \( m \cdot \Delta x \) for any change \( \Delta x \) in input

Quadratic Functions: Linear Rate of Change

A quadratic function \( f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c \) has a rate of change that is itself a linear function. Over equal-length intervals, the average rate of change changes by a constant amount.

Specifically, for consecutive intervals of length \( h \), the second differences (differences of the AROC values) are constant and equal to \( 2a \cdot h \).

Secant Lines and Slope

The secant line through two points on a graph has slope equal to the average rate of change between those points. For a linear function, every secant line has the same slope. For a quadratic, the secant line slope changes depending on which points you choose.

Concavity from Rate of Change

For a quadratic \( f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c \):

  • If \( a > 0 \): the rate of change is increasing, so the function is concave up
  • If \( a < 0 \): the rate of change is decreasing, so the function is concave down

Worked Example

Consider \( f(x) = 2x^2 - x + 3 \). Compute the AROC on \( [0, 1] \), \( [1, 2] \), and \( [2, 3] \):

  • \( f(0) = 3 \), \( f(1) = 4 \), \( f(2) = 9 \), \( f(3) = 18 \)
  • AROC on \( [0,1] = \frac{4-3}{1} = 1 \)
  • AROC on \( [1,2] = \frac{9-4}{1} = 5 \)
  • AROC on \( [2,3] = \frac{18-9}{1} = 9 \)

The AROCs are \( 1, 5, 9 \). The differences between consecutive AROCs are \( 5 - 1 = 4 \) and \( 9 - 5 = 4 \). The constant second difference \( 4 = 2(2)(1) = 2ah \) confirms this is quadratic with \( a = 2 \).

Key Idea: Linear functions have constant first differences over equal intervals. Quadratic functions have constant second differences over equal intervals.
AP Exam Tip: When given a table of values, check the second differences to determine if data could be modeled by a quadratic function. Equal spacing in \( x \)-values is required for this test to work.
