problem_sets.title: Practice: Sinusoidal Function Context and Data Modeling

problems.question_html: The depth of water in a harbor varies sinusoidally. The maximum depth is 14 feet and the minimum depth is 6 feet. What is the amplitude of the depth function?

hints.text: Amplitude \( = \frac{\text{max} - \text{min}}{2} \).

solution_steps.text: The water depth varies 4 feet above and below the midline.

problems.question_html: A Ferris wheel has a diameter of 40 meters and its center is 25 meters above the ground. A rider boards at the lowest point. What is the midline of the rider's height function?

hints.text: The midline corresponds to the center height of the Ferris wheel.
The center is 25 meters above the ground, so the midline is \( y = 25 \).

solution_steps.text: The midline of the height function equals the height of the Ferris wheel's center: 25 meters.
The rider's height oscillates between \( 25 - 20 = 5 \) m (bottom) and \( 25 + 20 = 45 \) m (top).

problems.question_html: The average temperature in a city reaches its maximum of \( 92^\circ\text{F} \) in month 7 and its minimum of \( 48^\circ\text{F} \) in month 1. What is the midline temperature?

hints.text: The midline is the average of the maximum and minimum.

problems.question_html: A tide completes one full cycle every 12.4 hours. What is \( b \) in the sinusoidal model \( h(t) = a\sin(bt) + d \)? Round to three decimal places.

hints.text: Use \( b = \frac{2\pi}{\text{period}} \).

problems.question_html:
A city records the following average monthly temperatures (in \( ^\circ\text{F} \)):

Month14710
Temp30558055

Which sinusoidal model best fits this data?

hints.text: Find amplitude, midline, period, and where the max occurs.
Amplitude \( = \frac{80-30}{2} = 25 \), midline \( = 55 \), period \( = 12 \) (so \( b = \frac{\pi}{6} \)), max at \( t = 7 \).

solution_steps.text: Max \( = 80 \), min \( = 30 \). Amplitude \( = 25 \), midline \( = 55 \). Period \( = 12 \), so \( b = \frac{\pi}{6} \).
Max at \( t = 7 \): cosine form with shift 7. \( T(t) = 25\cos\!\left(\frac{\pi}{6}(t-7)\right) + 55 \).

problems.question_html: In the sinusoidal temperature model \( T(t) = 22\cos\!\left(\frac{\pi}{6}(t - 7)\right) + 63 \), what does the value 22 represent in context?

choices.text: The temperature varies by \( 22^\circ\text{F} \) above and below the average of \( 63^\circ\text{F} \)
The period of the temperature cycle is 22 months
The lowest temperature occurs in month 22

hints.text: The coefficient in front of cosine is the amplitude. What does amplitude mean in this context?
The amplitude 22 means the temperature fluctuates \( 22^\circ\text{F} \) above and below the midline of \( 63^\circ\text{F} \).

solution_steps.text: In \( T(t) = 22\cos(\ldots) + 63 \), the coefficient 22 is the amplitude.
In context, this means the average monthly temperature varies \( 22^\circ\text{F} \) above and below the annual average of \( 63^\circ\text{F} \).

problems.question_html: A Ferris wheel with radius 15 meters makes one complete revolution every 2 minutes. The bottom of the wheel is 3 meters above the ground. A rider boards at the bottom. Find the rider's height above the ground after 30 seconds.

hints.text: Set up the model: center height \( = 3 + 15 = 18 \), amplitude \( = 15 \), period \( = 2 \) min = 120 s. Since the rider starts at the bottom, use \( -\cos \).

solution_steps.text: Center height \( = 3 + 15 = 18 \) m. Amplitude \( = 15 \). Period \( = 120 \) s, so \( b = \frac{2\pi}{120} = \frac{\pi}{60} \).
Rider starts at bottom (minimum), so use \( h(t) = -15\cos\!\left(\frac{\pi}{60}t\right) + 18 \).

problems.question_html: A sinusoidal regression on tidal data gives \( h(t) = 3.2\sin(0.51t - 1.8) + 5.1 \), where \( h \) is in feet and \( t \) is in hours. Estimate the period of the tides. Round to one decimal place.

hints.text: The period is \( \frac{2\pi}{|b|} \). Identify \( b \) from the regression equation.
\( b = 0.51 \), so period \( = \frac{2\pi}{0.51} \approx 12.3 \) hours.

problems.question_html:
The number of daylight hours \( D \) in a city varies sinusoidally over the year. The longest day has 15 hours of daylight (June 21, day 172) and the shortest day has 9 hours (December 21, day 355).

(a) Find the amplitude, midline, and period of \( D(t) \), where \( t \) is the day of the year.

(b) Write a cosine model for \( D(t) \).

(c) Use your model to estimate the number of daylight hours on the spring equinox (approximately day 80). Does your answer make sense?
problems.correct_answer:
(a) Amplitude = (15-9)/2 = 3 hours. Midline = (15+9)/2 = 12 hours. Period = 365 days.
(b) b = 2π/365. Max at t = 172: D(t) = 3cos((2π/365)(t - 172)) + 12.
(c) D(80) = 3cos((2π/365)(80-172)) + 12 = 3cos((2π/365)(-92)) + 12 = 3cos(-1.583) + 12 ≈ 3(-0.0027) + 12 ≈ 11.99 ≈ 12 hours. This makes sense because the spring equinox has approximately equal day and night (12 hours each).

hints.text: The longest and shortest days give you the max and min. The period for daylight is one year (365 days).
Amplitude 3, midline 12, period 365. Cosine centered at max day 172. For the equinox, expect about 12 hours.

solution_steps.text: (c) \( D(80) = 3\cos\!\left(\frac{2\pi}{365}(80-172)\right) + 12 = 3\cos(-1.583) + 12 \approx 3(-0.003) + 12 \approx 12 \) hours. This is consistent with the equinox having nearly equal day and night.

problems.question_html:
An oceanographer collects the following tidal depth data (in feet) at a coastal location:

Time (hrs)036912
Depth (ft)4.28.04.20.44.2

(a) Explain why a sinusoidal model is appropriate for this data.

(b) Determine the amplitude, midline, period, and write a cosine model \( D(t) \).

(c) A boat needs at least 6 feet of water to safely dock. Using your model, estimate the time intervals during one cycle when the boat can dock.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) The data shows a repeating pattern: depth rises, falls, and returns to the same value (4.2) at regular intervals. This periodic behavior is characteristic of tidal patterns, which are well-modeled by sinusoidal functions.
(b) Max = 8.0, min = 0.4. Amplitude = (8.0-0.4)/2 = 3.8. Midline = (8.0+0.4)/2 = 4.2. Period = 12 hours (from t=0 to t=12, both at 4.2 with a full cycle). b = 2π/12 = π/6. Max at t=3: D(t) = 3.8cos((π/6)(t-3)) + 4.2.
(c) Solve 3.8cos((π/6)(t-3)) + 4.2 ≥ 6. cos((π/6)(t-3)) ≥ (6-4.2)/3.8 ≈ 0.4737. (π/6)(t-3) ≤ ±1.077. t-3 is between -2.06 and 2.06. So approximately t ∈ [0.94, 5.06]. The boat can dock roughly from hour 1 to hour 5 during each cycle.

hints.text: Note how the depth returns to 4.2 at \( t = 0 \), \( t = 6 \), and \( t = 12 \). Identify the full cycle.
Amplitude 3.8, midline 4.2, period 12, max at \( t = 3 \). For part (c), set \( D(t) \geq 6 \) and solve for \( t \).

solution_steps.text: (a) The data repeats: \( D(0) = D(6) = D(12) = 4.2 \), with a max of 8.0 and min of 0.4. This periodic pattern matches a sinusoidal model.

(c) Solve \( 3.8\cos\!\left(\frac{\pi}{6}(t-3)\right) + 4.2 \geq 6 \): \( \cos\!\left(\frac{\pi}{6}(t-3)\right) \geq 0.474 \). This gives \( \frac{\pi}{6}(t-3) \in [-1.077, 1.077] \), so \( t \in [0.94, 5.06] \). The boat can dock approximately from hour 1 to hour 5.

concepts.title: The Tangent Function
concepts.content_html:
The Tangent Function

The tangent function is defined as the ratio of sine to cosine:

\[ \tan(\theta) = \frac{\sin(\theta)}{\cos(\theta)} \]

This ratio gives tangent its unique behavior, including vertical asymptotes where cosine equals zero.

Graph of \( y = \tan(x) \)

The tangent function has distinct properties that set it apart from sine and cosine:

  • Period: \( \pi \) (not \( 2\pi \)). The tangent function repeats every \( \pi \) units.
  • Vertical asymptotes: At \( x = \frac{\pi}{2} + n\pi \) for any integer \( n \), because \( \cos(x) = 0 \) at these values.
  • Domain: All real numbers except \( x = \frac{\pi}{2} + n\pi \).
  • Range: \( (-\infty, \infty) \) — tangent has no maximum or minimum.
  • Zeros: At \( x = n\pi \) (where \( \sin(x) = 0 \)).
  • No amplitude: Since tangent has no bounded range, the concept of amplitude does not apply.

Behavior Near Asymptotes

As \( x \) approaches \( \frac{\pi}{2} \) from the left, \( \sin(x) \to 1 \) and \( \cos(x) \to 0^+ \), so \( \tan(x) \to +\infty \). As \( x \) approaches \( \frac{\pi}{2} \) from the right, \( \cos(x) \to 0^- \), so \( \tan(x) \to -\infty \).

Transformations of \( y = \tan(x) \)

The general form \( f(x) = a\tan(b(x - h)) + k \) involves:

  • \( a \): vertical stretch (and reflection if \( a < 0 \))
  • \( b \): changes the period to \( \frac{\pi}{|b|} \)
  • \( h \): horizontal shift (phase shift)
  • \( k \): vertical shift

The vertical asymptotes shift accordingly. For \( y = \tan(bx) \), asymptotes occur at \( x = \frac{\pi}{2|b|} + \frac{n\pi}{|b|} \).

Worked Example

Find the period and vertical asymptotes of \( f(x) = \tan(2x) \).

  • Period: \( \frac{\pi}{|b|} = \frac{\pi}{2} \)
  • Asymptotes of \( \tan(\theta) \) at \( \theta = \frac{\pi}{2} + n\pi \). Set \( 2x = \frac{\pi}{2} + n\pi \), so \( x = \frac{\pi}{4} + \frac{n\pi}{2} \).
  • First few asymptotes: \( x = \ldots, -\frac{\pi}{4}, \frac{\pi}{4}, \frac{3\pi}{4}, \ldots \)
Key Idea: The tangent function increases throughout each period (between consecutive asymptotes). There is an inflection point (zero of the standard tangent) at the midpoint between consecutive asymptotes.
AP Exam Tip: Remember that \( \tan(x) \) is undefined at \( x = \frac{\pi}{2} + n\pi \). On the AP exam, if asked for the domain, exclude these values explicitly.

problems.question_html: What is the period of \( y = \tan(x) \)?

hints.text: Unlike sine and cosine, the tangent function repeats over a shorter interval.
The period of \( \tan(x) \) is \( \pi \).

solution_steps.text: The tangent function satisfies \( \tan(x + \pi) = \tan(x) \) for all \( x \) in its domain.

problems.question_html: At which value of \( x \) does \( y = \tan(x) \) have a vertical asymptote?

hints.text: Vertical asymptotes occur where \( \cos(x) = 0 \).
\( \cos\!\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) = 0 \), so \( \tan\!\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) \) is undefined.

solution_steps.text: \( \cos(x) = 0 \) at \( x = \frac{\pi}{2} + n\pi \). The answer \( x = \frac{\pi}{2} \) is one such value.
The tangent function has a zero at \( x = 0 \).

problems.question_html: The range of \( y = \tan(x) \) is __________.

hints.text: Unlike sine and cosine, tangent is unbounded. It can take any value.
The range is all real numbers: \( (-\infty, \infty) \).

solution_steps.text: As \( x \) approaches a vertical asymptote, \( \tan(x) \to \pm\infty \).
The range of \( \tan(x) \) is \( (-\infty, \infty) \), or all real numbers.

problems.question_html: What is the period of \( f(x) = \tan(3x) \)?

hints.text: The period of \( \tan(bx) \) is \( \frac{\pi}{|b|} \).
Period \( = \frac{\pi}{3} \).

solution_steps.text: For \( \tan(bx) \), the period is \( \frac{\pi}{|b|} \). Here \( b = 3 \).

problems.question_html: Which of the following describes the graph of \( g(x) = -\tan(x) + 2 \)?

choices.text: Reflected over the \( x \)-axis with vertical asymptotes at \( x = n\pi \)
Reflected over the \( x \)-axis and shifted up 2, with vertical asymptotes at \( x = \frac{\pi}{2} + n\pi \)

hints.text: The negative sign reflects the graph. The \( +2 \) shifts it up. What about the asymptotes?
The asymptotes are unchanged (still at \( \frac{\pi}{2} + n\pi \)). The graph is reflected (decreasing between asymptotes) and shifted up 2.

solution_steps.text: \( -\tan(x) \) reflects the tangent graph over the midline (now decreasing between asymptotes).
\( +2 \) shifts the graph up by 2. The asymptotes remain at \( x = \frac{\pi}{2} + n\pi \).

problems.question_html: Find the vertical asymptotes of \( h(x) = \tan\!\left(2\!\left(x - \frac{\pi}{4}\right)\right) \) that are nearest to \( x = 0 \). Enter both values separated by a comma, with the smaller value first.

hints.text: Set the argument equal to \( \frac{\pi}{2} + n\pi \) and solve for \( x \).

\( 2\!\left(x - \frac{\pi}{4}\right) = \frac{\pi}{2} + n\pi \). Solve: \( x = \frac{\pi}{4} + \frac{\pi}{4} + \frac{n\pi}{2} = \frac{\pi}{2} + \frac{n\pi}{2} \). For \( n = -1 \): \( x = 0 \). For \( n = 0 \): \( x = \frac{\pi}{2} \).

solution_steps.text: Set \( 2\!\left(x - \frac{\pi}{4}\right) = \frac{\pi}{2} + n\pi \). Solving: \( x - \frac{\pi}{4} = \frac{\pi}{4} + \frac{n\pi}{2} \), so \( x = \frac{\pi}{2} + \frac{n\pi}{2} \).
For \( n = -1 \): \( x = 0 \). For \( n = 0 \): \( x = \frac{\pi}{2} \). These are the asymptotes nearest to the origin.

hints.text: Find the reference angle for \( \frac{5\pi}{4} \) and determine the sign of tangent in that quadrant.
Reference angle: \( \frac{5\pi}{4} - \pi = \frac{\pi}{4} \). In QIII, tangent is positive. \( \tan\!\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) = 1 \).

solution_steps.text: \( \frac{5\pi}{4} \) is in Quadrant III. Reference angle: \( \frac{5\pi}{4} - \pi = \frac{\pi}{4} \).

problems.question_html:
Consider the function \( f(x) = 2\tan\!\left(\frac{x}{2}\right) - 1 \).

(a) Find the period of \( f \).

(b) Find the equations of the vertical asymptotes on the interval \( (-2\pi, 2\pi) \).

(c) Find the zeros of \( f \) on the interval \( (-2\pi, 2\pi) \) and describe the behavior of \( f \) between consecutive asymptotes.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) Period = π/|b| = π/(1/2) = 2π.
(b) Set x/2 = π/2 + nπ, so x = π + 2nπ. On (-2π, 2π): x = -π and x = π.
(c) Zeros: set 2tan(x/2) - 1 = 0, so tan(x/2) = 1/2. x/2 = arctan(1/2) + nπ. x = 2arctan(1/2) + 2nπ ≈ 0.927 + 2nπ. On (-2π, 2π): x ≈ 0.927 and x ≈ 0.927 - 2π ≈ -5.36 (outside interval). So x ≈ 0.927 is the only zero. Between consecutive asymptotes, f increases from -∞ to +∞, shifted down 1 and stretched vertically by 2.

hints.text: For \( \tan(bx) \), the period is \( \frac{\pi}{|b|} \). Identify \( b \) here.
\( b = \frac{1}{2} \), so period \( = 2\pi \). Asymptotes where \( \frac{x}{2} = \frac{\pi}{2} + n\pi \), i.e., \( x = \pi + 2n\pi \).

solution_steps.text: (b) \( \frac{x}{2} = \frac{\pi}{2} + n\pi \Rightarrow x = \pi + 2n\pi \). On \( (-2\pi, 2\pi) \): \( x = -\pi \) and \( x = \pi \).

(c) Zeros: \( 2\tan\!\left(\frac{x}{2}\right) = 1 \Rightarrow \tan\!\left(\frac{x}{2}\right) = \frac{1}{2} \Rightarrow x = 2\arctan\!\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) \approx 0.927 \). Between \( x = -\pi \) and \( x = \pi \), \( f \) increases from \( -\infty \) to \( +\infty \), crossing the \( x \)-axis at \( x \approx 0.927 \).

problems.question_html:
A student is analyzing the function \( g(x) = \tan\!\left(\frac{\pi x}{4}\right) \).

(a) Find the period and the vertical asymptotes.

(b) Evaluate \( g(1) \) and \( g(2) \).

(c) Explain why the tangent function has no amplitude, and describe how the vertical stretch factor \( a \) in \( a\tan(bx) \) affects the graph differently than the amplitude of a sine function.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) b = π/4. Period = π/(π/4) = 4. Asymptotes: (π/4)x = π/2 + nπ, so x = 2 + 4n. Asymptotes at x = ..., -2, 2, 6, ...
(b) g(1) = tan(π/4) = 1. g(2) = tan(π/2), which is undefined (vertical asymptote).
(c) The tangent function has range (-∞, ∞), so there is no maximum or minimum, and amplitude (which measures the displacement from midline to max) does not apply. The vertical stretch factor a in a·tan(bx) changes the steepness of the curve: larger |a| makes the graph steeper near the zero, but the function still approaches ±∞ near asymptotes regardless of a.

hints.text: Use \( \text{period} = \frac{\pi}{|b|} \) with \( b = \frac{\pi}{4} \). For asymptotes, set the argument equal to \( \frac{\pi}{2} + n\pi \).
Period \( = \frac{\pi}{\pi/4} = 4 \). Asymptotes at \( x = 2 + 4n \). Note that \( g(2) \) is at an asymptote.

solution_steps.text: (c) Amplitude requires bounded max/min values. Since \( \tan(x) \) has range \( (-\infty, \infty) \), there is no amplitude. The factor \( a \) controls steepness: \( a\tan(bx) \) stretches output values but does not bound them.

concepts.title: Inverse Trigonometric Functions
concepts.content_html:
Inverse Trigonometric Functions

Trigonometric functions are not one-to-one on their entire domains, so to define inverse functions we must restrict the domain of each trig function to an interval where it is strictly monotonic (always increasing or always decreasing).

The Three Principal Inverse Trig Functions

Arcsine: \( y = \arcsin(x) \) is the inverse of \( y = \sin(x) \) restricted to \( \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right] \).

  • Domain: \( -1 \leq x \leq 1 \)
  • Range: \( -\dfrac{\pi}{2} \leq y \leq \dfrac{\pi}{2} \)

Arccosine: \( y = \arccos(x) \) is the inverse of \( y = \cos(x) \) restricted to \( [0,\, \pi] \).

  • Domain: \( -1 \leq x \leq 1 \)
  • Range: \( 0 \leq y \leq \pi \)

Arctangent: \( y = \arctan(x) \) is the inverse of \( y = \tan(x) \) restricted to \( \left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \).

  • Domain: all real numbers
  • Range: \( -\dfrac{\pi}{2} < y < \dfrac{\pi}{2} \)
Key Idea: The output of an inverse trig function is an angle. For \( \arcsin \) and \( \arctan \), that angle lies in Quadrants I or IV. For \( \arccos \), it lies in Quadrants I or II.

Evaluating Inverse Trig Functions

To evaluate \( \arcsin\!\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) \), ask: "What angle \( \theta \) in \( \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right] \) satisfies \( \sin(\theta) = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \)?" The answer is \( \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{3} \).

Compositions of Trig and Inverse Trig

When a trig function is composed with its own inverse, cancellation occurs only when the input falls in the restricted domain:

  • \( \sin(\arcsin(x)) = x \) for \( -1 \leq x \leq 1 \)
  • \( \arcsin(\sin(\theta)) = \theta \) only when \( \theta \in \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right] \)

Worked Example

Find \( \arccos\!\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \).

We need \( \theta \in [0,\, \pi] \) with \( \cos(\theta) = -\dfrac{1}{2} \). Since cosine is negative in Quadrant II, the reference angle is \( \dfrac{\pi}{3} \), giving \( \theta = \pi - \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{2\pi}{3} \).

AP Exam Tip: A common error is writing \( \arcsin(\sin(\pi)) = \pi \). Since \( \pi \) is outside the range \( \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right] \), you must find the equivalent angle in that interval: \( \arcsin(\sin(\pi)) = \arcsin(0) = 0 \).

Using Inverse Trig to Solve for Angles

If \( \cos(\theta) = 0.6 \) and \( 0 \leq \theta \leq \pi \), then \( \theta = \arccos(0.6) \approx 0.927 \) radians. Technology (a calculator in radian mode) gives decimal approximations when exact values are not available.

problems.question_html: What is the value of \( \arcsin\!\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \)?

hints.text: Find the angle in \( \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right] \) whose sine equals \( \dfrac{1}{2} \).
\( \sin\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2} \), and \( \dfrac{\pi}{6} \) is in the range of arcsine.

problems.question_html: What is the value of \( \arccos\!\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right) \)?

hints.text: The range of arccosine is \( [0, \pi] \). Which angle in that interval has cosine equal to \( -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \)?
The reference angle for cosine \( \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \) is \( \dfrac{\pi}{4} \). Since cosine is negative, the angle is in Quadrant II: \( \pi - \dfrac{\pi}{4} = \dfrac{3\pi}{4} \).

solution_steps.text: The reference angle is \( \dfrac{\pi}{4} \). In Quadrant II, \( \theta = \pi - \dfrac{\pi}{4} = \dfrac{3\pi}{4} \).

problems.question_html: Evaluate \( \arctan(1) \). Give your answer as an exact fraction of \( \pi \) (e.g., enter pi/6).

hints.text: Which angle in \( \left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \) has tangent equal to 1?
\( \tan\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = 1 \).

problems.question_html: Evaluate \( \arcsin\!\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) \). Give your answer as an exact fraction of \( \pi \) (e.g., enter -pi/6).

hints.text: The range of arcsine includes negative angles. Which angle in \( \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right] \) has sine equal to \( -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \)?
\( \sin\!\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \).

problems.question_html: What is the value of \( \arcsin\!\left(\sin\!\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right)\right) \)?

hints.text: First compute \( \sin\!\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right) \), then apply arcsine. Remember arcsine's range.
\( \sin\!\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2} \). Then \( \arcsin\!\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{6} \).

solution_steps.text: Note: \( \dfrac{5\pi}{6} \) is outside the range of arcsine, so \( \arcsin(\sin(\theta)) \neq \theta \) here.

problems.question_html: Which expression equals \( \cos(\arctan(3)) \)?

hints.text: Let \( \theta = \arctan(3) \). Draw a right triangle with opposite side 3 and adjacent side 1. What is the hypotenuse?
Hypotenuse \( = \sqrt{1^2 + 3^2} = \sqrt{10} \). So \( \cos(\theta) = \dfrac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \).

solution_steps.text: Construct a right triangle: opposite = 3, adjacent = 1, hypotenuse = \( \sqrt{1 + 9} = \sqrt{10} \).

problems.question_html: If \( \arccos(x) = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \), what is the value of \( x \)?

hints.text: If \( \arccos(x) = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \), then \( \cos\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = x \).
\( \cos\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \).

solution_steps.text: Since \( \arccos(x) = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \), applying cosine to both sides gives \( x = \cos\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) \).

problems.question_html: Find the exact value of \( \tan(\arcsin(-0.6)) \). Express your answer as a fraction (e.g., -3/4).

hints.text: Let \( \theta = \arcsin(-0.6) \). Then \( \sin(\theta) = -0.6 = -\dfrac{3}{5} \). Use a right triangle to find \( \cos(\theta) \).
Adjacent side = \( \sqrt{5^2 - 3^2} = 4 \). Since \( \theta \) is negative (QIV), \( \cos(\theta) = \dfrac{4}{5} \). So \( \tan(\theta) = \dfrac{-3/5}{4/5} = -\dfrac{3}{4} \).

problems.question_html:
A 20-foot ladder leans against a building. The base of the ladder is 8 feet from the building.

(a) Write an expression using an inverse trigonometric function for the angle \( \theta \) the ladder makes with the ground.

(b) Evaluate \( \theta \) to the nearest hundredth of a radian.

(c) If the base is moved to 12 feet from the building, does \( \theta \) increase or decrease? Justify your answer.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) \( \theta = \arccos\!\left(\dfrac{8}{20}\right) = \arccos(0.4) \)
(b) \( \theta \approx 1.16 \) radians
(c) \( \theta \) decreases. Moving the base farther from the building increases the adjacent side relative to the hypotenuse, making \( \cos(\theta) \) larger. Since arccosine is a decreasing function, a larger input produces a smaller angle.

hints.text: For part (a), identify which side is adjacent to the angle and which is the hypotenuse. Use the appropriate inverse trig function.
Adjacent = 8, hypotenuse = 20, so \( \cos(\theta) = \dfrac{8}{20} \). For (b), use a calculator: \( \arccos(0.4) \approx 1.16 \). For (c), think about how arccosine behaves as its input increases.

solution_steps.text: (a) The adjacent side to \( \theta \) is 8 ft and the hypotenuse is 20 ft, so \( \theta = \arccos\!\left(\dfrac{8}{20}\right) = \arccos(0.4) \).
(c) When the base moves to 12 ft, \( \cos(\theta) = \dfrac{12}{20} = 0.6 \). Since \( 0.6 > 0.4 \) and arccosine is decreasing, the angle decreases. Intuitively, the ladder becomes less steep.

problems.question_html:
Consider the function \( g(x) = \arcsin(2x - 1) \).

(a) Find the domain of \( g \).

(b) Find the range of \( g \).

(c) Evaluate \( g(1) \) exactly.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) We need \( -1 \leq 2x - 1 \leq 1 \), which gives \( 0 \leq x \leq 1 \). Domain: \( [0, 1] \).
(b) Arcsine always outputs values in \( \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right] \). Since \( 2x - 1 \) covers \( [-1, 1] \) as \( x \) ranges over \( [0, 1] \), the range is \( \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right] \).
(c) \( g(1) = \arcsin(2(1) - 1) = \arcsin(1) = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \).

hints.text: For (a), arcsine requires its input to be between \( -1 \) and \( 1 \). Set up the inequality \( -1 \leq 2x - 1 \leq 1 \).
Solving: \( 0 \leq x \leq 1 \). For (b), as \( x \) goes from 0 to 1, \( 2x - 1 \) goes from \( -1 \) to 1, so arcsine covers its full range. For (c), plug in \( x = 1 \).

solution_steps.text: (a) The input to arcsine must satisfy \( -1 \leq 2x - 1 \leq 1 \). Adding 1: \( 0 \leq 2x \leq 2 \). Dividing by 2: \( 0 \leq x \leq 1 \).

(b) Since \( 2x - 1 \) takes all values in \( [-1, 1] \) over the domain, and arcsine maps \( [-1, 1] \) onto \( \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right] \), the range is \( \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right] \).

concepts.title: Trigonometric Equations and Inequalities
concepts.content_html:
Trigonometric Equations and Inequalities

Solving trigonometric equations means finding all angle values that make the equation true. Because trig functions are periodic, most trig equations have infinitely many solutions unless the domain is restricted.

Strategy for Solving Trig Equations

  1. Isolate the trig expression (get \( \sin(\theta) \), \( \cos(\theta) \), or \( \tan(\theta) \) alone on one side).
  2. Find the reference angle using inverse trig functions or known values.
  3. Identify all angles in \( [0, 2\pi) \) that satisfy the equation, using the sign of the trig value to determine the correct quadrants.
  4. Write the general solution by adding full-period multiples: \( \theta + 2\pi n \) for sine/cosine or \( \theta + \pi n \) for tangent, where \( n \) is any integer.
Key Idea: Because \( \sin \) and \( \cos \) have period \( 2\pi \) and \( \tan \) has period \( \pi \), general solutions repeat with those periods.

Worked Example 1: Solving \( 2\sin(\theta) - 1 = 0 \)

Step 1: Isolate sine: \( \sin(\theta) = \dfrac{1}{2} \).

Step 2: Reference angle: \( \arcsin\!\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{6} \).

Step 3: Sine is positive in Quadrants I and II, giving \( \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6} \) and \( \theta = \pi - \dfrac{\pi}{6} = \dfrac{5\pi}{6} \).

Step 4: General solution: \( \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6} + 2\pi n \) or \( \theta = \dfrac{5\pi}{6} + 2\pi n \), for any integer \( n \).

Worked Example 2: Domain-Restricted Solutions

Solve \( \cos(\theta) = -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \) for \( 0 \leq \theta < 2\pi \).

Reference angle: \( \dfrac{\pi}{6} \). Cosine is negative in QII and QIII.

Solutions: \( \theta = \dfrac{5\pi}{6} \) and \( \theta = \dfrac{7\pi}{6} \).

Using Technology

When exact values are not available (e.g., \( \sin(\theta) = 0.3 \)), use a calculator to find the reference angle \( \arcsin(0.3) \approx 0.3047 \), then determine all solutions in the desired interval.

Trigonometric Inequalities

To solve an inequality like \( \sin(\theta) > \dfrac{1}{2} \) on \( [0, 2\pi) \), first find where \( \sin(\theta) = \dfrac{1}{2} \) (at \( \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6} \) and \( \theta = \dfrac{5\pi}{6} \)), then determine where the graph of sine lies above \( \dfrac{1}{2} \). The solution is \( \dfrac{\pi}{6} < \theta < \dfrac{5\pi}{6} \).

AP Exam Tip: Always check whether the problem asks for solutions in a specific interval (like \( [0, 2\pi) \)) or the general solution. Giving a general solution when a restricted domain is specified, or vice versa, will lose credit.

problems.question_html: How many solutions does \( \sin(\theta) = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \) have on the interval \( [0, 2\pi) \)?

hints.text: In which quadrants is sine positive?
Sine is positive in Quadrants I and II. The solutions are \( \dfrac{\pi}{4} \) and \( \dfrac{3\pi}{4} \).

solution_steps.text: Sine is positive in QI and QII, giving \( \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \) and \( \theta = \pi - \dfrac{\pi}{4} = \dfrac{3\pi}{4} \). That is 2 solutions.

problems.question_html: Solve \( \tan(\theta) = -1 \) for \( 0 \leq \theta < 2\pi \). Which values of \( \theta \) are solutions?

hints.text: Tangent is negative in Quadrants II and IV. The reference angle for \( \tan(\theta) = 1 \) is \( \dfrac{\pi}{4} \).
QII: \( \pi - \dfrac{\pi}{4} = \dfrac{3\pi}{4} \). QIV: \( 2\pi - \dfrac{\pi}{4} = \dfrac{7\pi}{4} \).

solution_steps.text: Tangent is negative in QII and QIV: \( \theta = \dfrac{3\pi}{4} \) and \( \theta = \dfrac{7\pi}{4} \).

problems.question_html: Solve \( 2\cos(\theta) + 1 = 0 \) for \( 0 \leq \theta < 2\pi \). How many solutions are there?

hints.text: First isolate cosine: \( \cos(\theta) = -\dfrac{1}{2} \). In which quadrants is cosine negative?
Cosine is negative in QII and QIII. Reference angle \( \dfrac{\pi}{3} \) gives \( \theta = \dfrac{2\pi}{3} \) and \( \theta = \dfrac{4\pi}{3} \).

solution_steps.text: Cosine is negative in QII and QIII: \( \theta = \dfrac{2\pi}{3} \) and \( \theta = \dfrac{4\pi}{3} \). There are 2 solutions.

problems.question_html: Write the general solution to \( \tan(\theta) = \sqrt{3} \). Express your answer in the form \( \theta = a + bn \) where \( a \) is a fraction of \( \pi \) and \( b \) involves \( \pi \). Enter the value of \( a \) as a fraction of \( \pi \) (e.g., pi/3).

hints.text: Which angle has tangent equal to \( \sqrt{3} \)?
\( \tan\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = \sqrt{3} \). Since tangent has period \( \pi \), the general solution is \( \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{3} + \pi n \).

solution_steps.text: The general solution for tangent equations is \( \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{3} + \pi n \), where \( n \) is any integer.

problems.question_html: Solve \( 2\sin^2(\theta) - \sin(\theta) - 1 = 0 \) for \( 0 \leq \theta < 2\pi \). Which of the following is the complete solution set?

hints.text: Let \( u = \sin(\theta) \). Factor the quadratic \( 2u^2 - u - 1 = 0 \).

\( (2u + 1)(u - 1) = 0 \), so \( u = -\dfrac{1}{2} \) or \( u = 1 \). Solve each: \( \sin(\theta) = 1 \) gives \( \dfrac{\pi}{2} \); \( \sin(\theta) = -\dfrac{1}{2} \) gives \( \dfrac{7\pi}{6} \) and \( \dfrac{11\pi}{6} \).

problems.question_html: Solve \( \cos(2\theta) = \dfrac{1}{2} \) for \( 0 \leq \theta < 2\pi \). How many solutions does this equation have?

hints.text: Let \( \phi = 2\theta \). Since \( 0 \leq \theta < 2\pi \), we have \( 0 \leq \phi < 4\pi \). Solve \( \cos(\phi) = \dfrac{1}{2} \) on \( [0, 4\pi) \).

\( \cos(\phi) = \dfrac{1}{2} \) at \( \phi = \dfrac{\pi}{3}, \dfrac{5\pi}{3} \) in \( [0, 2\pi) \). Adding \( 2\pi \): also at \( \dfrac{7\pi}{3}, \dfrac{11\pi}{3} \). That gives 4 values of \( \phi \), hence 4 values of \( \theta \).

solution_steps.text: Dividing each by 2: \( \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6},\, \dfrac{5\pi}{6},\, \dfrac{7\pi}{6},\, \dfrac{11\pi}{6} \). There are 4 solutions.

problems.question_html: On the interval \( [0, 2\pi) \), for how many values of \( \theta \) is \( \cos(\theta) \leq -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \) true?

hints.text: This is an inequality, not an equation. The solution will be an interval (or union of intervals), not isolated points.

\( \cos(\theta) = -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \) at \( \theta = \dfrac{5\pi}{6} \) and \( \theta = \dfrac{7\pi}{6} \). The cosine curve is at or below \( -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \) for \( \dfrac{5\pi}{6} \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{7\pi}{6} \), which contains infinitely many values.

solution_steps.text: Cosine is at or below \( -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \) on the interval \( \left[\dfrac{5\pi}{6},\, \dfrac{7\pi}{6}\right] \).
Since this is a continuous interval, it contains infinitely many values of \( \theta \).

problems.question_html: Find the solution interval for \( \sin(\theta) > \dfrac{1}{2} \) on \( [0, 2\pi) \). Express the endpoints as fractions of \( \pi \) (e.g., pi/6). Enter the lower bound only.

hints.text: First find where \( \sin(\theta) = \dfrac{1}{2} \) on \( [0, 2\pi) \). The inequality holds between those boundary values.
\( \sin(\theta) = \dfrac{1}{2} \) at \( \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6} \) and \( \theta = \dfrac{5\pi}{6} \). Sine exceeds \( \dfrac{1}{2} \) on \( \left(\dfrac{\pi}{6},\, \dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right) \).

solution_steps.text: Since sine is above \( \dfrac{1}{2} \) between these values, the solution is \( \dfrac{\pi}{6} < \theta < \dfrac{5\pi}{6} \). The lower bound is \( \dfrac{\pi}{6} \).

problems.question_html:
A Ferris wheel has a radius of 30 feet with its center 40 feet above the ground. A rider's height \( h \) in feet after \( t \) seconds is modeled by \( h(t) = 40 - 30\cos\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{15}t\right) \).

(a) Find all times \( t \) in the interval \( [0, 60] \) when the rider is exactly 55 feet above the ground.

(b) Write the inequality that represents when the rider is above 55 feet, and solve it for \( t \in [0, 60] \).

(c) For what total amount of time during \( [0, 60] \) is the rider above 55 feet?
problems.correct_answer:
(a) Set \( 40 - 30\cos\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{15}t\right) = 55 \). Then \( \cos\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{15}t\right) = -\dfrac{1}{2} \). Let \( u = \dfrac{\pi}{15}t \). \( \cos(u) = -\dfrac{1}{2} \) at \( u = \dfrac{2\pi}{3} + 2\pi n \) and \( u = \dfrac{4\pi}{3} + 2\pi n \). Converting back: \( t = 10, 20, 40, 50 \) seconds.
(b) \( 40 - 30\cos\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{15}t\right) > 55 \) simplifies to \( \cos\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{15}t\right) < -\dfrac{1}{2} \). Solutions: \( 10 < t < 20 \) and \( 40 < t < 50 \).
(c) Each interval has length 10 seconds, and there are 2 intervals, so the rider is above 55 feet for a total of 20 seconds.

hints.text: For (a), set \( h(t) = 55 \) and isolate the cosine term. Determine the values of \( \dfrac{\pi}{15}t \) that work.
\( \cos\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{15}t\right) = -\dfrac{1}{2} \). The period of the cosine argument is \( 2\pi \div \dfrac{\pi}{15} = 30 \) seconds. Find solutions in \( [0, 60] \) (two full periods).

solution_steps.text: (b) \( h(t) > 55 \) requires \( \cos\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{15}t\right) < -\dfrac{1}{2} \), which holds for \( 10 < t < 20 \) and \( 40 < t < 50 \).

problems.question_html:
Consider the equation \( \sin(\theta) + \cos(\theta) = 1 \).

(a) Find all solutions on \( [0, 2\pi) \) by squaring both sides. Identify and reject any extraneous solutions.

(b) Verify your solutions by substituting back into the original equation.

(c) Explain why squaring can introduce extraneous solutions in trigonometric equations.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) Squaring: \( \sin^2(\theta) + 2\sin(\theta)\cos(\theta) + \cos^2(\theta) = 1 \). Using \( \sin^2 + \cos^2 = 1 \): \( 1 + 2\sin(\theta)\cos(\theta) = 1 \), so \( \sin(2\theta) = 0 \). Then \( 2\theta = 0, \pi, 2\pi, 3\pi \), giving \( \theta = 0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \pi, \dfrac{3\pi}{2} \).
Check each: \( \theta = 0 \): \( 0 + 1 = 1 \) (valid). \( \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \): \( 1 + 0 = 1 \) (valid). \( \theta = \pi \): \( 0 + (-1) = -1 \neq 1 \) (extraneous). \( \theta = \dfrac{3\pi}{2} \): \( -1 + 0 = -1 \neq 1 \) (extraneous).
Solutions: \( \theta = 0 \) and \( \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \).
(b) \( \sin(0) + \cos(0) = 0 + 1 = 1 \). \( \sin\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) + \cos\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = 1 + 0 = 1 \). Both verified.
(c) Squaring is not a reversible operation. If \( a = b \), then \( a^2 = b^2 \), but \( a^2 = b^2 \) only implies \( a = \pm b \). Squaring effectively adds the equation \( \sin(\theta) + \cos(\theta) = -1 \), whose solutions become extraneous.

hints.text: After squaring, use the Pythagorean identity and the double-angle identity \( 2\sin(\theta)\cos(\theta) = \sin(2\theta) \).
You should get \( \sin(2\theta) = 0 \), giving 4 candidate solutions. Check each in the original equation: two will fail.

solution_steps.text: Check: \( \theta = 0 \) and \( \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \) satisfy the original equation. \( \theta = \pi \) and \( \theta = \dfrac{3\pi}{2} \) give \( -1 \) (extraneous).
(c) Squaring loses sign information, introducing solutions of \( \sin\theta + \cos\theta = -1 \) as extraneous solutions.

concepts.title: The Secant, Cosecant, and Cotangent Functions
concepts.content_html:
The Secant, Cosecant, and Cotangent Functions

The three reciprocal trigonometric functions are defined in terms of sine, cosine, and tangent:

  • \( \csc(\theta) = \dfrac{1}{\sin(\theta)} \) (cosecant is the reciprocal of sine)
  • \( \sec(\theta) = \dfrac{1}{\cos(\theta)} \) (secant is the reciprocal of cosine)
  • \( \cot(\theta) = \dfrac{1}{\tan(\theta)} = \dfrac{\cos(\theta)}{\sin(\theta)} \) (cotangent is the reciprocal of tangent)

Domains

Each reciprocal function is undefined wherever its "parent" function equals zero:

  • \( \csc(\theta) \) is undefined when \( \sin(\theta) = 0 \), i.e., at \( \theta = n\pi \) for any integer \( n \).
  • \( \sec(\theta) \) is undefined when \( \cos(\theta) = 0 \), i.e., at \( \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2} + n\pi \).
  • \( \cot(\theta) \) is undefined when \( \sin(\theta) = 0 \), i.e., at \( \theta = n\pi \).

Ranges

  • \( \csc(\theta) \): \( (-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty) \)
  • \( \sec(\theta) \): \( (-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty) \)
  • \( \cot(\theta) \): \( (-\infty, \infty) \)
Key Idea: The graphs of \( \csc(\theta) \) and \( \sec(\theta) \) never cross the horizontal band \( -1 < y < 1 \). Vertical asymptotes occur at every zero of the parent function.

Graph Features

Cosecant: Vertical asymptotes at \( \theta = n\pi \). U-shaped curves open upward where \( \sin > 0 \) and downward where \( \sin < 0 \). Period: \( 2\pi \).

Secant: Vertical asymptotes at \( \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2} + n\pi \). U-shaped curves open upward where \( \cos > 0 \) and downward where \( \cos < 0 \). Period: \( 2\pi \).

Cotangent: Vertical asymptotes at \( \theta = n\pi \). Decreasing on each interval \( (n\pi, (n+1)\pi) \). Period: \( \pi \).

Worked Example

Evaluate \( \sec\!\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right) \).

Since \( \sec(\theta) = \dfrac{1}{\cos(\theta)} \), we compute \( \cos\!\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right) = -\dfrac{1}{2} \). Therefore \( \sec\!\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right) = \dfrac{1}{-1/2} = -2 \).

Relationship Summary

FunctionReciprocal ofPeriod
\( \csc(\theta) \)\( \sin(\theta) \)\( 2\pi \)
\( \sec(\theta) \)\( \cos(\theta) \)\( 2\pi \)
\( \cot(\theta) \)\( \tan(\theta) \)\( \pi \)
AP Exam Tip: Do not confuse \( \csc(\theta) \) with \( \sin^{-1}(\theta) \). Cosecant is the reciprocal (\( 1/\sin \)), while \( \sin^{-1} \) (arcsine) is the inverse function. They are completely different.
concepts.content_raw: The Secant, Cosecant, and Cotangent Functions

problem_sets.title: Practice: The Secant, Cosecant, and Cotangent Functions

problems.question_html: What is the value of \( \csc\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) \)?

hints.text: Cosecant is the reciprocal of sine. What is \( \sin\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) \)?
\( \sin\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2} \), so \( \csc\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = \dfrac{1}{1/2} = 2 \).

solution_steps.text: Cosecant is the reciprocal of sine: \( \csc(\theta) = \dfrac{1}{\sin(\theta)} \).

problems.question_html: The function \( y = \sec(x) \) has vertical asymptotes at which values of \( x \)?

choices.text: \( x = n\pi \) for any integer \( n \)
\( x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} + n\pi \) for any integer \( n \)

hints.text: Secant is undefined where its parent function equals zero. Which function is that?
\( \sec(x) = \dfrac{1}{\cos(x)} \), so asymptotes occur where \( \cos(x) = 0 \), which is at \( x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} + n\pi \).

solution_steps.text: \( \cos(x) = 0 \) at \( x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} + n\pi \), where \( n \) is any integer.

problems.question_html: What is the period of the cotangent function \( y = \cot(x) \)? Enter an exact value involving \( \pi \) (e.g., 2pi).

hints.text: Cotangent is the reciprocal of tangent. What is the period of tangent?
Tangent has period \( \pi \), and cotangent shares the same period: \( \pi \).

solution_steps.text: The cotangent function \( \cot(x) = \dfrac{\cos(x)}{\sin(x)} \) repeats every \( \pi \) units.

problems.question_html: Evaluate \( \sec(\pi) \).

hints.text: \( \sec(\pi) = \dfrac{1}{\cos(\pi)} \). What is \( \cos(\pi) \)?

solution_steps.text: Secant is the reciprocal of cosine: \( \sec(\theta) = \dfrac{1}{\cos(\theta)} \).

problems.question_html: If \( \csc(\theta) = -\dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{3} \) and \( \pi < \theta < \dfrac{3\pi}{2} \), what is \( \cos(\theta) \)?

hints.text: First find \( \sin(\theta) \) from the cosecant value. Then use \( \sin^2(\theta) + \cos^2(\theta) = 1 \).
\( \sin(\theta) = \dfrac{1}{\csc(\theta)} = -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \). Then \( \cos^2(\theta) = 1 - \dfrac{3}{4} = \dfrac{1}{4} \). In QIII, cosine is negative, so \( \cos(\theta) = -\dfrac{1}{2} \).

problems.question_html: Which of the following best describes the graph of \( y = \csc(x) \) on the interval \( (0, \pi) \)?

choices.text: A U-shaped curve opening downward with a minimum at \( x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \)
A U-shaped curve opening upward with a minimum at \( x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \)

hints.text: On \( (0, \pi) \), sine is positive, so cosecant is also positive. What happens as sine approaches 0 from above?

As \( x \to 0^+ \) or \( x \to \pi^- \), \( \sin(x) \to 0^+ \), so \( \csc(x) \to +\infty \). The minimum of \( \csc(x) \) occurs where \( \sin(x) \) is maximum: at \( x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \) with \( \csc = 1 \).

solution_steps.text: \( \csc(x) \to +\infty \) near both asymptotes (\( x = 0 \) and \( x = \pi \)).
The minimum value is \( \csc\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = 1 \). The curve forms a U-shape opening upward.

problems.question_html: Evaluate \( \cot\!\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{4}\right) \).

hints.text: \( \cot(\theta) = \dfrac{\cos(\theta)}{\sin(\theta)} \). Find sine and cosine of \( \dfrac{5\pi}{4} \).
\( \sin\!\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{4}\right) = -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \) and \( \cos\!\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{4}\right) = -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \). So \( \cot = \dfrac{-\sqrt{2}/2}{-\sqrt{2}/2} = 1 \).

solution_steps.text: \( \dfrac{5\pi}{4} \) is in QIII with reference angle \( \dfrac{\pi}{4} \).

problems.question_html: If \( \sec(\theta) = 3 \), what is the value of \( \cos(\theta) \)? Express as a fraction.

hints.text: Secant and cosine are reciprocals of each other.
\( \cos(\theta) = \dfrac{1}{\sec(\theta)} = \dfrac{1}{3} \).

problems.question_html:
Consider the function \( f(x) = 2\csc(x) - 1 \) on the interval \( (0, 2\pi) \).

(a) State the equations of all vertical asymptotes of \( f \) on this interval.

(b) Find the local minimum value of \( f \) and the \( x \)-value where it occurs.

(c) Find the local maximum value of \( f \) and the \( x \)-value where it occurs.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) Vertical asymptotes at \( x = \pi \) (the only zero of sine in the open interval \( (0, 2\pi) \); \( x = 0 \) and \( x = 2\pi \) are excluded from the domain interval).
(b) On \( (0, \pi) \), \( \csc(x) \geq 1 \), so \( f(x) = 2\csc(x) - 1 \geq 2(1) - 1 = 1 \). The local minimum value is 1, occurring at \( x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \).
(c) On \( (\pi, 2\pi) \), \( \csc(x) \leq -1 \), so \( f(x) = 2\csc(x) - 1 \leq 2(-1) - 1 = -3 \). The local maximum value is \( -3 \), occurring at \( x = \dfrac{3\pi}{2} \).

hints.text: Vertical asymptotes of \( \csc(x) \) occur where \( \sin(x) = 0 \). For (b) and (c), the extreme values of \( \csc(x) \) occur at the peaks and troughs of \( \sin(x) \).

On \( (0, \pi) \), \( \csc(x) \) has its minimum value of 1 at \( x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \). On \( (\pi, 2\pi) \), \( \csc(x) \) has its maximum value of \( -1 \) at \( x = \dfrac{3\pi}{2} \). Apply the transformation \( 2\csc(x) - 1 \).

solution_steps.text: (a) \( \sin(x) = 0 \) at \( x = \pi \) within \( (0, 2\pi) \). So the only vertical asymptote is \( x = \pi \).
(b) On \( (0, \pi) \), \( \sin(x) \) reaches its max of 1 at \( x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \), so \( \csc \) reaches its min of 1. \( f\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = 2(1) - 1 = 1 \).

(c) On \( (\pi, 2\pi) \), \( \sin(x) \) reaches its min of \( -1 \) at \( x = \dfrac{3\pi}{2} \), so \( \csc = -1 \). \( f\!\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right) = 2(-1) - 1 = -3 \). This is a local maximum for the lower branch.

problems.question_html:
A student claims that the range of \( y = \sec(x) \) is \( (-\infty, -1) \cup (1, \infty) \).

(a) Is this claim correct? If not, state the correct range.

(b) Explain why \( \sec(x) \) can never take values in the interval \( (-1, 1) \).

(c) Can \( \sec(x) \) equal exactly 1 or \( -1 \)? If so, give one \( x \)-value for each.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) The claim is incorrect. The correct range is \( (-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty) \), using closed brackets because \( \sec(x) \) can equal 1 and \( -1 \).
(b) Since \( \cos(x) \) has range \( [-1, 1] \), and \( \sec(x) = 1/\cos(x) \), when \( |\cos(x)| \leq 1 \) (and nonzero), we get \( |\sec(x)| = 1/|\cos(x)| \geq 1 \). So \( \sec(x) \) can never be between \( -1 \) and 1.
(c) Yes. \( \sec(0) = 1/\cos(0) = 1/1 = 1 \). \( \sec(\pi) = 1/\cos(\pi) = 1/(-1) = -1 \).

hints.text: Check whether \( \sec(x) \) can actually equal 1 or \( -1 \). What value of \( \cos(x) \) would produce those outputs?
\( \sec(x) = 1 \) when \( \cos(x) = 1 \) (at \( x = 0 \)). \( \sec(x) = -1 \) when \( \cos(x) = -1 \) (at \( x = \pi \)). So the range includes the endpoints.

solution_steps.text: (a) The range should use closed brackets: \( (-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty) \). The student's open intervals exclude 1 and \( -1 \), which are achievable values.

concepts.title: Equivalent Representations of Trigonometric Functions
concepts.content_html:
Equivalent Representations of Trigonometric Functions

Trigonometric identities allow us to rewrite expressions in equivalent forms. On the AP Precalculus exam, three families of identities are assessed: Pythagorean identities, sum and difference identities (for sine and cosine only), and double-angle identities (for sine and cosine only).

Pythagorean Identities

These follow directly from the unit circle definition \( \cos^2(\theta) + \sin^2(\theta) = 1 \):

  • \( \sin^2(\theta) + \cos^2(\theta) = 1 \)
  • \( 1 + \tan^2(\theta) = \sec^2(\theta) \) (divide the first by \( \cos^2(\theta) \))
  • \( 1 + \cot^2(\theta) = \csc^2(\theta) \) (divide the first by \( \sin^2(\theta) \))

Sum and Difference Identities

For any angles \( \alpha \) and \( \beta \):

  • \( \sin(\alpha + \beta) = \sin(\alpha)\cos(\beta) + \cos(\alpha)\sin(\beta) \)
  • \( \sin(\alpha - \beta) = \sin(\alpha)\cos(\beta) - \cos(\alpha)\sin(\beta) \)
  • \( \cos(\alpha + \beta) = \cos(\alpha)\cos(\beta) - \sin(\alpha)\sin(\beta) \)
  • \( \cos(\alpha - \beta) = \cos(\alpha)\cos(\beta) + \sin(\alpha)\sin(\beta) \)
Key Idea: Notice the sign pattern: in the cosine identities, the sign in the result is opposite to the sign in the argument. In the sine identities, the sign is the same.

Double-Angle Identities

Setting \( \alpha = \beta = \theta \) in the sum identities gives:

  • \( \sin(2\theta) = 2\sin(\theta)\cos(\theta) \)
  • \( \cos(2\theta) = \cos^2(\theta) - \sin^2(\theta) \)

Using the Pythagorean identity, the double-angle formula for cosine can also be written as:

  • \( \cos(2\theta) = 2\cos^2(\theta) - 1 \)
  • \( \cos(2\theta) = 1 - 2\sin^2(\theta) \)

Worked Example

Find the exact value of \( \cos(75^\circ) \).

Write \( 75^\circ = 45^\circ + 30^\circ \). Then:

\[ \cos(75^\circ) = \cos(45^\circ)\cos(30^\circ) - \sin(45^\circ)\sin(30^\circ) = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \cdot \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} - \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{\sqrt{6} - \sqrt{2}}{4} \]

AP Exam Tip: Half-angle identities, tangent sum/difference identities, and product-to-sum identities are NOT assessed on the AP Precalculus exam. Focus only on Pythagorean, sum/difference (sin and cos), and double-angle (sin and cos) identities.

problem_sets.title: Practice: Equivalent Representations of Trigonometric Functions

problems.question_html: Which expression is equivalent to \( \sin^2(\theta) \)?

hints.text: Use the fundamental Pythagorean identity \( \sin^2(\theta) + \cos^2(\theta) = 1 \).
Solving for \( \sin^2(\theta) \): \( \sin^2(\theta) = 1 - \cos^2(\theta) \).

problems.question_html: What is the exact value of \( \sin(75^\circ) \)?

hints.text: Write \( 75^\circ = 45^\circ + 30^\circ \) and apply the sine sum identity.

\( \sin(75^\circ) = \sin(45^\circ)\cos(30^\circ) + \cos(45^\circ)\sin(30^\circ) = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \cdot \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{\sqrt{6} + \sqrt{2}}{4} \).

problems.question_html: Simplify: \( \cos^2(\theta) - \sin^2(\theta) \). Write your answer using a double-angle expression (e.g., cos(2theta)).

hints.text: This expression appears in one of the double-angle identities.
\( \cos(2\theta) = \cos^2(\theta) - \sin^2(\theta) \).

problems.question_html: Use the double-angle identity to find \( \sin(2\theta) \) if \( \sin(\theta) = \dfrac{3}{5} \) and \( \cos(\theta) = \dfrac{4}{5} \). Express as a fraction.

hints.text: The double-angle identity is \( \sin(2\theta) = 2\sin(\theta)\cos(\theta) \).
\( \sin(2\theta) = 2 \cdot \dfrac{3}{5} \cdot \dfrac{4}{5} = \dfrac{24}{25} \).

problems.question_html: Which expression is equivalent to \( \cos(\alpha - \beta) \)?

hints.text: In the cosine difference identity, the sign in the result is opposite to the sign in the argument.
\( \cos(\alpha - \beta) = \cos(\alpha)\cos(\beta) + \sin(\alpha)\sin(\beta) \). The minus in the argument becomes a plus in the formula.

solution_steps.text: The sign flips: a minus in the argument yields a plus in the expanded form.

problems.question_html: If \( \cos(\theta) = \dfrac{5}{13} \) and \( \theta \) is in Quadrant IV, what is \( \cos(2\theta) \)?

hints.text: Use \( \cos(2\theta) = 2\cos^2(\theta) - 1 \). You do not need \( \sin(\theta) \) for this form.

problems.question_html: Find the exact value of \( \cos(15^\circ) \). Express your answer in the form \( \dfrac{\sqrt{a} + \sqrt{b}}{4} \). Enter the value of \( a + b \).

hints.text: Write \( 15^\circ = 45^\circ - 30^\circ \) and apply the cosine difference identity.
\( \cos(15^\circ) = \cos(45^\circ)\cos(30^\circ) + \sin(45^\circ)\sin(30^\circ) = \dfrac{\sqrt{6} + \sqrt{2}}{4} \). So \( a = 6 \) and \( b = 2 \), giving \( a + b = 8 \).

problems.question_html: Simplify \( \dfrac{\sin(2\theta)}{1 + \cos(2\theta)} \) to a single trigonometric function of \( \theta \). Enter your answer (e.g., tan(theta)).

hints.text: Replace \( \sin(2\theta) \) with \( 2\sin(\theta)\cos(\theta) \) and \( \cos(2\theta) \) with \( 2\cos^2(\theta) - 1 \).

Numerator: \( 2\sin\theta\cos\theta \). Denominator: \( 1 + 2\cos^2\theta - 1 = 2\cos^2\theta \). So the fraction becomes \( \dfrac{2\sin\theta\cos\theta}{2\cos^2\theta} = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = \tan\theta \).

problems.question_html:
Given that \( \sin(\alpha) = \dfrac{4}{5} \) with \( \alpha \) in QI, and \( \cos(\beta) = -\dfrac{5}{13} \) with \( \beta \) in QII:

(a) Find \( \cos(\alpha) \) and \( \sin(\beta) \).

(b) Find the exact value of \( \sin(\alpha + \beta) \).

(c) Find the exact value of \( \cos(\alpha - \beta) \).

hints.text: Use the Pythagorean identity to find the missing trig values. Pay attention to sign based on quadrant.
\( \cos(\alpha) = \sqrt{1 - 16/25} = \dfrac{3}{5} \). \( \sin(\beta) = \sqrt{1 - 25/169} = \dfrac{12}{13} \). Then apply sum/difference identities.

problems.question_html:
Prove the identity \( \dfrac{\sin(2\theta)}{\sin(\theta)} - \dfrac{\cos(2\theta)}{\cos(\theta)} = \sec(\theta) \).

(a) Rewrite the left side using double-angle identities.

(b) Simplify the expression step by step.

(c) Show that the simplified result equals \( \sec(\theta) \).

hints.text: Replace \( \sin(2\theta) \) with \( 2\sin\theta\cos\theta \) and \( \cos(2\theta) \) with \( \cos^2\theta - \sin^2\theta \). Simplify each fraction separately.
After simplifying: first term becomes \( 2\cos\theta \). Combine over common denominator \( \cos\theta \), then use the Pythagorean identity in the numerator.

concepts.title: Trigonometry and Polar Coordinates
concepts.content_html:
Trigonometry and Polar Coordinates

The polar coordinate system locates points in the plane using a distance and an angle rather than horizontal and vertical distances. A point is described by the ordered pair \( (r, \theta) \), where \( r \) is the signed radius (directed distance from the origin) and \( \theta \) is the angle measured counterclockwise from the positive \( x \)-axis.

Signed Radius Values

When \( r > 0 \), the point lies on the terminal ray of the angle \( \theta \) at distance \( r \) from the origin. When \( r < 0 \), the point lies on the ray opposite the terminal ray of \( \theta \), at distance \( |r| \) from the origin.

Key Idea: A negative \( r \)-value does not mean the point is "negative distance" from the origin. It means the point is reflected through the origin: \( (-r, \theta) \) is the same point as \( (r, \theta + \pi) \).

Converting Between Rectangular and Polar Coordinates

Polar to Rectangular:

  • \( x = r\cos(\theta) \)
  • \( y = r\sin(\theta) \)

Rectangular to Polar:

  • \( r = \pm\sqrt{x^2 + y^2} \) (choose sign based on quadrant and desired \( \theta \))
  • \( \tan(\theta) = \dfrac{y}{x} \) (adjust \( \theta \) for the correct quadrant)

Worked Example 1: Polar to Rectangular

Convert \( \left(4, \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) \) to rectangular coordinates.

\( x = 4\cos\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = 4 \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} = 2 \)

\( y = 4\sin\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = 4 \cdot \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 2\sqrt{3} \)

The rectangular coordinates are \( (2, 2\sqrt{3}) \).

Worked Example 2: Negative \( r \)

Plot the point \( (-3, \dfrac{\pi}{4}) \) in polar coordinates.

First, face the direction \( \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \). Since \( r = -3 \), move 3 units in the opposite direction. This places the point in QIII, equivalent to \( (3, \dfrac{5\pi}{4}) \).

Multiple Representations

Every point in polar coordinates has infinitely many representations. Adding \( 2\pi \) to \( \theta \) gives the same point: \( (r, \theta) = (r, \theta + 2\pi) \). Also, \( (r, \theta) = (-r, \theta + \pi) \).

AP Exam Tip: When converting from rectangular to polar, remember to check the quadrant. Using \( \theta = \arctan\!\left(\dfrac{y}{x}\right) \) alone may give the wrong quadrant because arctangent only returns values in \( \left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \).

problems.question_html: Convert the polar point \( \left(6, \dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) \) to rectangular coordinates. What is the \( x \)-coordinate?

hints.text: Use \( x = r\cos(\theta) \).
\( x = 6\cos\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = 6 \cdot \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 3\sqrt{3} \).

solution_steps.text: Use the conversion formula \( x = r\cos(\theta) \).

problems.question_html: The polar point \( (-2, \dfrac{\pi}{2}) \) is equivalent to which point with a positive \( r \)?

hints.text: To convert a negative \( r \) to positive, add \( \pi \) to the angle.

problems.question_html: Convert the rectangular point \( (1, 1) \) to polar coordinates. What is \( r \)?

hints.text: Use \( r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} \).

solution_steps.text: Use the conversion formula \( r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} \).

problems.question_html: Convert the rectangular point \( (-1, \sqrt{3}) \) to polar coordinates. What is \( \theta \) (in radians, with \( r > 0 \) and \( 0 \leq \theta < 2\pi \))? Enter as a fraction of \( \pi \).

hints.text: The point \( (-1, \sqrt{3}) \) is in QII. Find \( \arctan\!\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{-1}\right) \) and adjust for the correct quadrant.
\( \arctan(-\sqrt{3}) = -\dfrac{\pi}{3} \). Since the point is in QII, add \( \pi \): \( \theta = -\dfrac{\pi}{3} + \pi = \dfrac{2\pi}{3} \).

solution_steps.text: The point \( (-1, \sqrt{3}) \) is in QII. Reference angle: \( \arctan\!\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{1}\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{3} \).

problems.question_html: Convert the polar point \( \left(5, \dfrac{5\pi}{3}\right) \) to rectangular coordinates. What are \( (x, y) \)?

hints.text: Use \( x = r\cos\theta \) and \( y = r\sin\theta \). Note that \( \dfrac{5\pi}{3} \) is in QIV.
\( \cos\!\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{3}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2} \) and \( \sin\!\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{3}\right) = -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \). So \( x = \dfrac{5}{2} \), \( y = -\dfrac{5\sqrt{3}}{2} \).

problems.question_html: Which rectangular equation corresponds to the polar equation \( r = 4\cos(\theta) \)?

hints.text: Multiply both sides by \( r \) to get \( r^2 = 4r\cos(\theta) \). What are \( r^2 \) and \( r\cos(\theta) \) in rectangular?

solution_steps.text: Multiply both sides of \( r = 4\cos\theta \) by \( r \): \( r^2 = 4r\cos\theta \).
Substitute: \( x^2 + y^2 = 4x \). (This is a circle of radius 2 centered at \( (2, 0) \).)

problems.question_html: Convert the rectangular point \( (0, -5) \) to polar coordinates with \( r > 0 \) and \( 0 \leq \theta < 2\pi \). What is \( \theta \) (as a fraction of \( \pi \))?

hints.text: The point \( (0, -5) \) is on the negative \( y \)-axis. What angle corresponds to the negative \( y \)-axis?
\( r = 5 \), \( \theta = \dfrac{3\pi}{2} \) (pointing straight down).

solution_steps.text: The point is on the negative \( y \)-axis, so \( \theta = \dfrac{3\pi}{2} \).

problems.question_html: The polar point \( \left(3, \dfrac{7\pi}{4}\right) \) is the same as \( \left(-3, \theta\right) \) for some \( \theta \in [0, 2\pi) \). Find \( \theta \) as a fraction of \( \pi \).

hints.text: To switch the sign of \( r \), add or subtract \( \pi \) from the angle.

problems.question_html:
A radar station detects an aircraft at polar coordinates \( (120, \dfrac{5\pi}{6}) \) where \( r \) is in kilometers.

(a) Convert these coordinates to rectangular (Cartesian) form.

(b) How far west of the station is the aircraft?

(c) Another aircraft is detected at \( (-80, \dfrac{11\pi}{6}) \). Convert this to rectangular coordinates and determine which aircraft is farther from the station.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) \( x = 120\cos\!\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right) = 120\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = -60\sqrt{3} \approx -103.9 \) km. \( y = 120\sin\!\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right) = 120 \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} = 60 \) km. Rectangular: \( (-60\sqrt{3}, 60) \).
(b) The aircraft is \( 60\sqrt{3} \approx 103.9 \) km west (the \( x \)-coordinate is negative, indicating west).
(c) \( x = -80\cos\!\left(\dfrac{11\pi}{6}\right) = -80 \cdot \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = -40\sqrt{3} \). \( y = -80\sin\!\left(\dfrac{11\pi}{6}\right) = -80 \cdot \left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = 40 \). Rectangular: \( (-40\sqrt{3}, 40) \). Distance from station: \( \sqrt{(-40\sqrt{3})^2 + 40^2} = \sqrt{4800 + 1600} = \sqrt{6400} = 80 \) km. The first aircraft (120 km) is farther.

hints.text: Use \( x = r\cos\theta \) and \( y = r\sin\theta \). For the negative \( r \), multiply through carefully.
First aircraft: \( (-60\sqrt{3}, 60) \) at distance 120 km. Second aircraft: \( (-40\sqrt{3}, 40) \) at distance 80 km.

solution_steps.text: (c) For \( (-80, 11\pi/6) \): \( x = -80\cos(11\pi/6) = -40\sqrt{3} \), \( y = -80\sin(11\pi/6) = 40 \). Distance = \( |r| = 80 \) km. First aircraft (120 km) is farther.

problems.question_html:
Consider the rectangular equation \( x^2 + y^2 - 6y = 0 \).

(a) Convert this equation to polar form.

(b) Identify the graph as a circle and give its center and radius in rectangular coordinates.

(c) Explain why the polar form is simpler than the rectangular form for describing this curve.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) Substitute \( x^2 + y^2 = r^2 \) and \( y = r\sin\theta \): \( r^2 - 6r\sin\theta = 0 \). Factor: \( r(r - 6\sin\theta) = 0 \). Since \( r = 0 \) is just the origin (included when \( \theta = 0 \)), the equation is \( r = 6\sin\theta \).
(b) Complete the square: \( x^2 + (y^2 - 6y + 9) = 9 \), so \( x^2 + (y - 3)^2 = 9 \). Center: \( (0, 3) \), radius: 3.
(c) The polar form \( r = 6\sin\theta \) is a single, clean equation directly giving \( r \) as a function of \( \theta \). The rectangular form requires completing the square and is longer. The polar form also makes it easy to plot the curve by evaluating \( r \) for various \( \theta \).

hints.text: Replace \( x^2 + y^2 \) with \( r^2 \) and \( y \) with \( r\sin\theta \). Factor out \( r \).
You get \( r = 6\sin\theta \). For (b), complete the square on the \( y \)-terms in the original equation.

solution_steps.text: (b) \( x^2 + y^2 - 6y = 0 \implies x^2 + (y - 3)^2 = 9 \). Circle with center \( (0, 3) \) and radius 3.
(c) The polar equation \( r = 6\sin\theta \) is a compact, explicit relationship. It reveals the structure (circle through the origin) more directly.

concepts.title: Polar Function Graphs
concepts.content_html:
Polar Function Graphs

A polar function has the form \( r = f(\theta) \), where the input is an angle and the output is a signed radius. As \( \theta \) varies, the point \( (f(\theta), \theta) \) traces a curve in the polar plane.

Key Polar Curves

Circles:

  • \( r = a \): circle centered at the origin with radius \( |a| \).
  • \( r = a\cos(\theta) \): circle of diameter \( |a| \), centered on the \( x \)-axis.
  • \( r = a\sin(\theta) \): circle of diameter \( |a| \), centered on the \( y \)-axis.

Cardioids: \( r = a \pm a\cos(\theta) \) or \( r = a \pm a\sin(\theta) \). These are heart-shaped curves that pass through the origin.

Lima\u00e7ons: \( r = a \pm b\cos(\theta) \) or \( r = a \pm b\sin(\theta) \), where \( a \neq b \). Depending on the ratio \( \dfrac{a}{b} \):

  • \( \dfrac{a}{b} < 1 \): inner loop
  • \( \dfrac{a}{b} = 1 \): cardioid (special case)
  • \( 1 < \dfrac{a}{b} < 2 \): dimpled
  • \( \dfrac{a}{b} \geq 2 \): convex

Rose Curves: \( r = a\cos(n\theta) \) or \( r = a\sin(n\theta) \).

  • If \( n \) is odd: \( n \) petals.
  • If \( n \) is even: \( 2n \) petals.
  • Each petal has length \( |a| \).
Key Idea: The output values of a polar function are signed radii, not just distances. When \( f(\theta) < 0 \), the point is plotted in the opposite direction from \( \theta \). A change in the sign of \( f(\theta) \) may correspond to no change in the actual distance from the origin if the point crosses through the origin.

Graphing Strategy

  1. Build a table of \( (\theta, r) \) values for key angles.
  2. Plot each point using the signed radius convention.
  3. Connect points smoothly, noting symmetry.

Worked Example

Graph \( r = 2 + 4\cos(\theta) \). Since \( a = 2 \) and \( b = 4 \), we have \( \dfrac{a}{b} = \dfrac{1}{2} < 1 \), so this is a lima\u00e7on with an inner loop.

Key points: At \( \theta = 0 \), \( r = 6 \). At \( \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \), \( r = 2 \). At \( \theta = \pi \), \( r = -2 \) (inner loop). At \( \theta = \dfrac{3\pi}{2} \), \( r = 2 \).

AP Exam Tip: When a polar function produces a negative \( r \)-value, the point is still plotted, but in the direction opposite to \( \theta \). Do not skip negative \( r \)-values when graphing; they often create inner loops or petals.

problems.question_html: The polar curve \( r = 3\cos(2\theta) \) is a rose. How many petals does it have?

hints.text: For \( r = a\cos(n\theta) \), the number of petals depends on whether \( n \) is odd or even.
When \( n \) is even, there are \( 2n \) petals. Here \( n = 2 \), so there are \( 2 \times 2 = 4 \) petals.

solution_steps.text: For \( r = a\cos(n\theta) \) with even \( n \), the rose has \( 2n \) petals.
Here \( n = 2 \), so the curve has \( 2(2) = 4 \) petals.

problems.question_html: Which type of polar curve is \( r = 3 + 3\sin(\theta) \)?

hints.text: Compare the coefficients: \( r = a + b\sin(\theta) \). What is \( \dfrac{a}{b} \)?
\( a = 3 \) and \( b = 3 \), so \( \dfrac{a}{b} = 1 \). This is a cardioid.

solution_steps.text: \( r = 3 + 3\sin(\theta) \) has the form \( r = a + b\sin(\theta) \) with \( a = b = 3 \).
When \( a = b \), the curve is a cardioid.

problems.question_html: How many petals does the rose curve \( r = 5\sin(3\theta) \) have?

hints.text: For \( r = a\sin(n\theta) \), the petal count depends on whether \( n \) is odd or even.
When \( n \) is odd, there are \( n \) petals. Here \( n = 3 \).

solution_steps.text: For \( r = a\sin(n\theta) \) with odd \( n \), there are \( n \) petals.
\( n = 3 \), so the rose has 3 petals.

problems.question_html: For the polar curve \( r = 1 + 3\cos(\theta) \), what is the value of \( r \) when \( \theta = \pi \)?

hints.text: Substitute \( \theta = \pi \) into \( r = 1 + 3\cos(\theta) \).

solution_steps.text: The negative value means the point is plotted opposite to the direction \( \theta = \pi \), which places it on the positive \( x \)-axis at distance 2.

problems.question_html: The polar curve \( r = 2 - 4\sin(\theta) \) has \( a = 2 \) and \( b = 4 \). Since \( \dfrac{a}{b} = \dfrac{1}{2} < 1 \), which feature does this curve have?

choices.text: It passes through the origin but has no loop

hints.text: When \( \dfrac{a}{b} < 1 \), the lima\u00e7on has a distinctive feature.
\( \dfrac{a}{b} < 1 \) produces an inner loop. The curve crosses the origin and loops back.

solution_steps.text: For \( r = a - b\sin\theta \) with \( \dfrac{a}{b} < 1 \), the curve is a lima\u00e7on with an inner loop.
Since \( \dfrac{2}{4} = \dfrac{1}{2} < 1 \), this curve has an inner loop.

problems.question_html: For the rose curve \( r = 4\cos(3\theta) \), what is the length of each petal?

hints.text: For \( r = a\cos(n\theta) \), each petal extends from the origin to a maximum distance. What is that maximum?
The maximum value of \( |r| \) is \( |a| = 4 \), which occurs when \( \cos(3\theta) = \pm 1 \).

solution_steps.text: Each petal of \( r = a\cos(n\theta) \) has length \( |a| \).
Here \( a = 4 \), so each petal has length 4.

problems.question_html: For the polar curve \( r = 4\sin(\theta) \), find \( r \) when \( \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6} \).

hints.text: Substitute \( \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6} \) into \( r = 4\sin(\theta) \).
\( r = 4\sin\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = 4 \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} = 2 \).

problems.question_html: The curve \( r = 5 + 2\cos(\theta) \) has \( a = 5 \) and \( b = 2 \). Since \( \dfrac{a}{b} = 2.5 \), which best describes the curve?

hints.text: Classify the lima\u00e7on based on the ratio \( \dfrac{a}{b} \).
\( \dfrac{a}{b} = 2.5 \geq 2 \), so the lima\u00e7on is convex (no dimple, no inner loop).

problems.question_html:
Consider the polar curve \( r = 2 + 4\cos(\theta) \).

(a) Classify this curve (type and any special features).

(b) Find the values of \( \theta \) in \( [0, 2\pi) \) where the curve passes through the origin.

(c) Find the maximum distance from the origin and the angle(s) where it occurs.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) \( r = a + b\cos\theta \) with \( a = 2, b = 4 \). \( \dfrac{a}{b} = \dfrac{1}{2} < 1 \), so this is a lima\u00e7on with an inner loop.
(b) Set \( r = 0 \): \( 2 + 4\cos\theta = 0 \implies \cos\theta = -\dfrac{1}{2} \implies \theta = \dfrac{2\pi}{3} \) and \( \theta = \dfrac{4\pi}{3} \).
(c) Maximum \( r \) occurs when \( \cos\theta = 1 \) (i.e., \( \theta = 0 \)): \( r = 2 + 4(1) = 6 \). The maximum distance from the origin is 6.

hints.text: Compare \( a \) and \( b \) to classify. For (b), set \( r = 0 \) and solve for \( \theta \).
\( \cos\theta = -\dfrac{1}{2} \) at \( \theta = \dfrac{2\pi}{3} \) and \( \dfrac{4\pi}{3} \). Maximum \( r \) occurs at \( \theta = 0 \) where \( \cos\theta \) is greatest.

solution_steps.text: (a) \( a = 2, b = 4, \dfrac{a}{b} = 0.5 < 1 \). This is a lima\u00e7on with an inner loop.
(c) \( r \) is maximized when \( \cos\theta = 1 \), at \( \theta = 0 \): \( r_{\max} = 2 + 4 = 6 \).

problems.question_html:
Consider the rose curve \( r = 3\sin(2\theta) \).

(a) How many petals does the curve have? Justify your answer.

(b) Find all values of \( \theta \) in \( [0, 2\pi) \) where the curve passes through the origin.

(c) In which quadrants are the petals located? Explain by analyzing the signs of \( r \) and the corresponding angles.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) Since \( n = 2 \) is even, the rose has \( 2n = 4 \) petals.
(b) \( r = 0 \) when \( \sin(2\theta) = 0 \), i.e., \( 2\theta = 0, \pi, 2\pi, 3\pi \), giving \( \theta = 0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \pi, \dfrac{3\pi}{2} \).
(c) For \( 0 < \theta < \dfrac{\pi}{2} \): \( \sin(2\theta) > 0 \), so \( r > 0 \), petal in QI. For \( \dfrac{\pi}{2} < \theta < \pi \): \( \sin(2\theta) < 0 \), so \( r < 0 \), point plotted opposite to \( \theta \), petal in QIV. For \( \pi < \theta < \dfrac{3\pi}{2} \): \( \sin(2\theta) > 0 \), \( r > 0 \), petal in QIII. For \( \dfrac{3\pi}{2} < \theta < 2\pi \): \( \sin(2\theta) < 0 \), \( r < 0 \), petal in QII. Petals are in all four quadrants.

hints.text: For the number of petals, use the even/odd rule for \( n \). For (b), set \( \sin(2\theta) = 0 \).
When \( r < 0 \), the petal appears opposite to the angle \( \theta \). Track the sign of \( r \) across each interval between zeros.

solution_steps.text: (a) \( n = 2 \) is even, so the rose has \( 2 \times 2 = 4 \) petals.
(c) Petals appear in all four quadrants. When \( r > 0 \), the petal is in the same quadrant as \( \theta \). When \( r < 0 \), the petal is reflected through the origin to the opposite quadrant.

concepts.title: Rates of Change in Polar Functions
concepts.content_html:
Rates of Change in Polar Functions

In polar functions of the form \( r = f(\theta) \), we can analyze how the signed radius \( r \) changes as the angle \( \theta \) changes. This is analogous to studying rates of change for Cartesian functions, but the input is an angle and the output is a signed radius value.

Average Rate of Change

The average rate of change of \( r = f(\theta) \) over the interval \( [\theta_1, \theta_2] \) is:

\[ \text{Average ROC} = \dfrac{f(\theta_2) - f(\theta_1)}{\theta_2 - \theta_1} \]

This measures how quickly the signed radius changes per unit change in the angle. The units are "units of \( r \) per radian."

Key Idea: The values \( f(\theta) \) are signed radius values, not distances from the origin. A positive rate of change means the signed radius is increasing (becoming more positive or less negative), which does not necessarily mean the point is moving farther from the origin.

Interpreting Rates of Change

Consider \( r = f(\theta) \). If \( f(\theta) \) is positive and increasing, the point is moving away from the origin. But if \( f(\theta) \) is negative and increasing (becoming less negative), the point might actually be moving closer to the origin, because \( |r| \) is decreasing.

When interpreting rates of change, use \( (f(\theta), \theta) \) notation for the point. For example: "As \( \theta \) increases from \( \dfrac{\pi}{4} \) to \( \dfrac{\pi}{2} \), the signed radius \( r \) decreases at an average rate of \( -2 \) per radian."

Worked Example

Let \( r = f(\theta) = 3 + 2\cos(\theta) \). Find the average rate of change of \( r \) from \( \theta = 0 \) to \( \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \).

\( f(0) = 3 + 2\cos(0) = 3 + 2 = 5 \)

\( f\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = 3 + 2\cos\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = 3 + 0 = 3 \)

\[ \text{Average ROC} = \dfrac{3 - 5}{\pi/2 - 0} = \dfrac{-2}{\pi/2} = -\dfrac{4}{\pi} \approx -1.27 \]

Interpretation: As \( \theta \) increases from \( 0 \) to \( \dfrac{\pi}{2} \), the signed radius decreases at an average rate of \( \dfrac{4}{\pi} \) per radian. Since \( r \) remains positive on this interval, the point is moving closer to the origin.

Positive vs. Negative Rates

  • Positive average ROC: \( r \) is increasing (signed radius becoming more positive).
  • Negative average ROC: \( r \) is decreasing (signed radius becoming more negative).
  • Zero average ROC: the signed radius has the same value at the start and end (but may change in between).
AP Exam Tip: When describing rates of change in polar functions, always specify that you are discussing the signed radius or the value of \( r = f(\theta) \), not the "distance from the origin." Changes in the signed radius do not always correspond to changes in distance from the origin, particularly when \( r \) changes sign.

problem_sets.title: Practice: Rates of Change in Polar Functions

problems.question_html: For \( r = f(\theta) = 4\sin(\theta) \), what is the average rate of change of \( r \) from \( \theta = 0 \) to \( \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6} \)?

hints.text: Compute \( f(0) \) and \( f(\pi/6) \), then use the average rate of change formula.

problems.question_html: For \( r = f(\theta) = 1 + 2\cos(\theta) \), the average rate of change from \( \theta = 0 \) to \( \theta = \pi \) is negative. What does this tell us about the signed radius?

choices.text: The signed radius increased on this interval.
The signed radius decreased on this interval (from a higher value to a lower value).
The point moved farther from the origin.

hints.text: A negative average rate of change means the output decreased overall from start to end.
\( f(0) = 3 \), \( f(\pi) = -1 \). The signed radius went from 3 to \( -1 \), a decrease.

solution_steps.text: A negative average ROC means \( f(\theta_2) < f(\theta_1) \), so the signed radius decreased.
Here \( f(0) = 3 \) and \( f(\pi) = -1 \), confirming the decrease from 3 to \( -1 \).

problems.question_html: For \( r = 2 + 3\sin(\theta) \), find the average rate of change from \( \theta = 0 \) to \( \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \). Express as a fraction involving \( \pi \).

hints.text: Compute \( f(0) \) and \( f(\pi/2) \), then divide the difference by \( \pi/2 \).

problems.question_html: For \( r = f(\theta) = 3\cos(\theta) \), find the average rate of change from \( \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{3} \) to \( \theta = \dfrac{2\pi}{3} \). Express as a fraction involving \( \pi \).

hints.text: Evaluate \( f \) at both endpoints and apply the average ROC formula.

problems.question_html: For the polar function \( r = f(\theta) = 2 - 4\sin(\theta) \), on which interval does the average rate of change equal zero?

hints.text: Average ROC equals zero when \( f(\theta_1) = f(\theta_2) \). Check which endpoints give the same \( r \)-value.
\( f(\pi/6) = 2 - 4(1/2) = 0 \) and \( f(5\pi/6) = 2 - 4(1/2) = 0 \). Same output, so average ROC = 0.

solution_steps.text: Since \( f(\pi/6) = f(5\pi/6) = 0 \), the average ROC is zero on \( \left[\dfrac{\pi}{6}, \dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right] \).

problems.question_html: For \( r = f(\theta) = 1 + 2\cos(\theta) \), the signed radius changes from \( f(\pi) = -1 \) to \( f\!\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right) = 1 \). A student concludes the point moved away from the origin. Is this correct?

choices.text: Yes, because \( r \) increased from \( -1 \) to 1.
No, because the distance from the origin is \( |r| \), which went from 1 to 1 (unchanged).
Yes, because a positive rate of change always means moving away from the origin.
No, because \( r \) must be positive for the point to exist.

hints.text: Signed radius and distance from the origin are related by \( d = |r| \). Check both \( |f(\pi)| \) and \( |f(3\pi/2)| \).
\( |f(\pi)| = |-1| = 1 \) and \( |f(3\pi/2)| = |1| = 1 \). The distance is the same; only the direction changed.

solution_steps.text: The signed radius increased from \( -1 \) to 1, but the distance from the origin is \( |r| \).
\( |{-1}| = 1 \) and \( |1| = 1 \). The distance from the origin did not change.
The student confused signed radius with distance. Increasing signed radius does not always mean increasing distance from the origin.

problems.question_html: For \( r = f(\theta) = 3 + \cos(\theta) \), find the average rate of change of \( r \) from \( \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \) to \( \theta = \pi \). Express as a fraction involving \( \pi \).

hints.text: Compute \( f(\pi/2) \) and \( f(\pi) \), then apply the formula.

problems.question_html: For \( r = f(\theta) = 4\cos(2\theta) \), find the average rate of change from \( \theta = 0 \) to \( \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \). Express as a fraction involving \( \pi \).

hints.text: Average ROC = \( \dfrac{0 - 4}{\pi/4 - 0} = \dfrac{-4}{\pi/4} = -\dfrac{16}{\pi} \).

problems.question_html:
The polar function \( r = f(\theta) = 2 + 3\sin(\theta) \) models the distance (in cm) from a sensor as a function of angle \( \theta \).

(a) Find the average rate of change of \( r \) from \( \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6} \) to \( \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \).

(b) Find the average rate of change from \( \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \) to \( \theta = \dfrac{5\pi}{6} \).

(c) Compare the two rates. Explain what this tells us about how the signed radius behaves on each interval.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) \( f(\pi/6) = 2 + 3(1/2) = 3.5 \). \( f(\pi/2) = 2 + 3(1) = 5 \). Average ROC = \( \dfrac{5 - 3.5}{\pi/2 - \pi/6} = \dfrac{1.5}{\pi/3} = \dfrac{4.5}{\pi} = \dfrac{9}{2\pi} \).
(b) \( f(5\pi/6) = 2 + 3(1/2) = 3.5 \). Average ROC = \( \dfrac{3.5 - 5}{5\pi/6 - \pi/2} = \dfrac{-1.5}{\pi/3} = -\dfrac{9}{2\pi} \).
(c) The rates are equal in magnitude but opposite in sign. On \( [\pi/6, \pi/2] \), the signed radius increases (moving away from the origin). On \( [\pi/2, 5\pi/6] \), the signed radius decreases at the same average rate (moving toward the origin). This symmetry reflects the fact that \( \sin(\theta) \) is symmetric about \( \theta = \pi/2 \).

hints.text: Evaluate \( f \) at \( \pi/6 \), \( \pi/2 \), and \( 5\pi/6 \). Notice the symmetry of sine about \( \pi/2 \).
Both intervals have width \( \pi/3 \). \( f(\pi/6) = f(5\pi/6) = 3.5 \) and \( f(\pi/2) = 5 \). The rates should be negatives of each other.

solution_steps.text: (c) The rates are \( \pm\dfrac{9}{2\pi} \). The signed radius increases then decreases symmetrically about \( \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \), reflecting the symmetry of sine.

problems.question_html:
Consider the cardioid \( r = f(\theta) = 1 - \cos(\theta) \).

(a) Find the average rate of change of \( r \) from \( \theta = 0 \) to \( \theta = \pi \).

(b) Find the average rate of change from \( \theta = \pi \) to \( \theta = 2\pi \).

(c) The signed radius at \( \theta = 0 \) and \( \theta = 2\pi \) is the same. Does this mean the average rate of change from \( 0 \) to \( 2\pi \) is zero? Verify, and explain what this means geometrically.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) \( f(0) = 1 - 1 = 0 \), \( f(\pi) = 1 - (-1) = 2 \). Average ROC = \( \dfrac{2 - 0}{\pi - 0} = \dfrac{2}{\pi} \).
(b) \( f(2\pi) = 1 - 1 = 0 \). Average ROC = \( \dfrac{0 - 2}{2\pi - \pi} = -\dfrac{2}{\pi} \).
(c) Yes, \( f(0) = f(2\pi) = 0 \), so the average ROC from \( 0 \) to \( 2\pi \) is \( \dfrac{0 - 0}{2\pi} = 0 \). Geometrically, the cardioid starts at the origin, expands outward to a maximum radius of 2 at \( \theta = \pi \), then contracts back to the origin. Over one full revolution, the net change in the signed radius is zero.

hints.text: Evaluate \( f \) at \( 0 \), \( \pi \), and \( 2\pi \). For (c), recall that zero average ROC does not mean the function was constant.
\( f(0) = 0 \), \( f(\pi) = 2 \), \( f(2\pi) = 0 \). Over a full revolution, the cardioid returns to its starting point.

solution_steps.text: (c) Over \( [0, 2\pi] \): average ROC = \( \dfrac{0 - 0}{2\pi} = 0 \). The curve traced a complete loop, returning to the origin. Zero net change does not mean \( r \) was constant; it means the increases and decreases canceled out.
